A `Requirement` is one edge of a ruleset's graph: a subject, a relation (`requires`, `excludedBy`, `obsoletedBy`, `replacedBy`, or one a plugin declares), its targets, how they combine and whose possession counts. `RequirementRegistry` holds a game's entries and registers the rules each owning package's deriver makes from them, under the entries' own ids, so play is unchanged. `replace` and `remove` change an entry and its rules together, and `for`/`leadsTo` read the graph either way for the civilopedia (civ-clone/web-renderer#37).
From the review of civ-clone/web-renderer#37's first batch:

`add` and `replace` check everything before changing anything: duplicate entry ids (including two replacements under one id), rule ids another rule already has, and entries that aren't entries. A plain object is taken as an entry, as a plugin might write one.

An entry owns the ids of the rules it made: replacing or removing it takes out whatever rule holds them by then, including one a plugin put in their place with `rules.replace`, so the last change wins.
`unregister` removes the entries it holds, by identity, and ignores others, like any registry.
Entries are frozen, since a ruleset's are shared by every game and its rules read them as they run.
`ruleRegistry()` says which rule registry the entries' rules go into.

core-rule 0.1.5 is the first with rule ids (`getById`, `DuplicateRuleIdError`), and the tests pass against 0.1.5 of both. Requiring ^0.1.6 put a second core-rule beside a tree that had settled on 0.1.5 (core-save-game's CI), so a game's rules and its requirements' were two different `RuleRegistry` classes.

`requirements` (core-game's new slot) is dispositioned `definitions`: plugin imports register its entries along with their rules, and play never changes them, so a load adopts it with `rules` and a save writes none of it (civ-clone/web-renderer#37).

localChanges: When a computer civilization loses its last city, it now comes back as one new civilization. Each unit the lost city had supported was bringing another one back, so a single defeat could add four or five civilizations at once, and a game could run out of civilizations to come back as within a few turns (closes #600).

log: When the city was its player's last, disbanding the first unit defeats the player, which destroys the rest; the loops over the city's supported units then destroyed each of those a second time, running every unit `Destroyed` rule again (civ-clone/web-renderer#600). Both loops now skip a unit that is already destroyed.

Losing its last city disbands the units the city supported, and each of those destroyed units checked whether its player was now defeated: the city had already changed hands, so every one of them processed `Defeated` for the same player, as did the capture itself afterwards, and civ1-game-end's respawn brought a civilization back for each (civ-clone/web-renderer#600). The three rules that defeat a player on losing a unit or a city now check, as their effect runs, that the player is still in the game, with the `PlayerRegistry` passed to them as to the `Defeated` rules. As their effect, not a criterion: a rule set's criteria are all evaluated before any of its effects run, and the disbanding that defeats the player first is an earlier effect of the same set.

Review of civ-clone/web-renderer#169:

`Disembark` leaves a stowed unit's `Stowed` busy state, and a busy unit is never active again, so raiders landed from a ship never moved: each is `activate()`d before it disembarks. Landing is also tried after sailing, not only before.

A ship whose best target was inland, or lay beside it with nowhere to land, floated for ever: it now sails for the best-scoring city it can reach a sea square beside (its own square excluded), and is removed when there is none.

A raider that captures a city stops and holds it, as one in its own city does; the leader stops on his friend's square instead of stepping off again; an enemy city next door is always entered, defended or not; only a plain `Move` counts as a step (an `Embark` extends `Move` and put raiders back aboard).
Scoring as v474.05: +4 onto any square but the unit's own city, +2 per axis that agrees with the way to the target (straight on +4).
`BuildRaiders` builds land units only (no Battleship, Bomber or Nuclear, which `Raid` can't use), the dearest attacker first as decision 3 says. The client keeps its dependencies for `actionFailed`.

New games and saved games now record which map grid the world is on, ready for isometric and hex maps. Nothing changes on screen yet, and games saved before this load as square, as they always have (closes #89).

log: The `start` rule reads the engine option `topologyId` (default `'square'`) and passes it to the generator as its `topologyId` option, which core-world-generator 0.1.7's `Generator.topology()` resolves through core-world's `createTopology` at the generator's final size; `World` 0.1.21 records the id from there.

Before generating, it validates the generator's own topology against the generator's own `width()` and `height()`, so an unknown id or a size the grid cannot make (an odd height on `staggered-iso` or `hex-odd-r`, which always wrap north to south) throws before any terrain is generated, rather than from inside `World`. Earth's maps are square data, so the `earth` option with any other `topologyId` throws an `Error` naming both, before a generator is picked.
Square worlds are unchanged: the generator's default grid is already square. core-world is now `^0.1.21` and core-world-generator `^0.1.7` (web-renderer#89).

Compile with `--force`, format as `npm run build` does, and fail if any `.js`, `.d.ts` or `.js.map` then differs from what is committed or was never added, as core-world-generator and simple-world-generator already do.

`Game.inject` rebuilt a loaded `World`'s transient `_generator` as a plain `new Generator(height, width)`, so its `topology()` was always square. With core-world 0.1.21 a world saves its grid as `_topologyId`, and with core-world-generator 0.1.7 a `Generator` takes a `topologyId` option, so the rebuild now passes `{ topologyId: target._topologyId ?? 'square' }` and the generator's `topology()`, `getNeighbours` and `distanceFrom` agree with the world it belongs to (civ-clone/web-renderer#89).

The id is read from the restored field, like the height and width. A world saved before ids were recorded has none when `fill` runs (`World.onHydrated`, which gives it `'square'`, runs afterwards), so its generator is square, as it always was. Nothing reads a loaded world's generator geometry today (`World.get` uses only `coordsToIndex`), so square worlds behave exactly as before; the comment above the rebuild no longer claims the geometry is a function of height and width alone.

The dependency ranges move to core-world ^0.1.21 and core-world-generator ^0.1.7, the first versions with `World._topologyId` and the `topologyId` option. Three inject tests: a loaded world saved as `'hex-odd-r'` gets a hex generator of its own size whose neighbours are the world topology's; a world saved without the field gets a square one; and no transient field of the world is left undefined.

`PlayerWorld` gains a `topologyId()` accessor, delegating to `World.topologyId()` (core-world 0.1.21), and a `topologyId` key, so the data a client is sent says which grid the world is on (civ-clone/web-renderer#89). The client never receives the `World` itself, only the player's view of it.

A save carries each object's keys beside its state, so a game saved before this would restore its `PlayerWorld`s without the key, never send it, and write the same keys into every later save. `onHydrated` adds the key when it is missing; `World` reports `'square'` for such a world.

core-world is now `^0.1.21`, for `World.topologyId()` and `TopologyId`. The package gets its first tests (mocha/chai/ts-mocha, as core-world's): the key is sent and reads `'square'` for a default world and `'hex-odd-r'`/`'staggered-iso'` for worlds whose generator was given those topologies, and a `PlayerWorld` restored with the old keys sends it after `onHydrated` (once, however often that runs).

The workflow is the standard one the other engine repos now use: pnpm on Node 22 with no lock file, `prettier --check`, a forced compile that fails on stale or uncommitted `.js`/`.d.ts`/`.js.map`, then the tests.

`prettier:check` gains `--check`: without it, it printed every file formatted and passed whatever their state. The unused `package-lock.json` (npm v2 lock from 0.1.13's era, pinning core-data-object 0.1.9 and no test tooling) is removed; CI resolves what a consumer would.
ITopology gains id(), returning a TopologyId: 'square', 'staggered-iso' or 'hex-odd-r'. These are written into saved games (web-renderer#89), so they are never renamed or reused.

topologies.ts exports createTopology(id, width, height), which builds and validates the topology an id names and throws a clear Error for an id it does not know, and topologyIds, the list. It is pure, so the UI can use it too. The staggered and hexagonal grids are always built to wrap north to south, as World.get does whatever the grid, so an odd height is refused for them rather than quietly making a world that does not wrap; square takes any size of at least 1 by 1.

A World takes the id of its generator's topology when it is built and keeps it in _topologyId, a saved (non-transient) field, with a topologyId() accessor. topology() is now built lazily from that id and the dimensions through createTopology, and is still transient and reset in onHydrated.
A world saved before the id was recorded has none: onHydrated makes it 'square', the only grid there was, so the next save records it.

A generator's topology from a copy of core-world older than id() (two copies exist whenever core-world-generator's core-world does not match, as in this package's own CI install) counts as square. The core-world-generator range is raised to ^0.1.6, the first with Generator.topology().

For a square world nothing plays differently. The one change a save shows is the new field: web-renderer's conformance state digest gains one field per checkpoint, and is otherwise unchanged (web-renderer#89).

A topology from a copy of core-world older than id() used to count as square whatever it was. That copy (0.1.20) already has StaggeredIsoTopology and HexOddRTopology, so one of those injected into a generator would have been saved as square. Class identity cannot be compared across copies, so the fallback now goes by class name: a SquareTopology, a generator's default, is still recorded as square, and anything else throws an Error naming the class and saying core-world-generator's copy of core-world predates topology ids.

`Object.freeze([dx, dy] as [number, number])` comes out as `readonly number[]` under TypeScript 4.8, which several engine checkouts pin, so `offset()`'s `Offset` return type rejected it (TS2322 in 20 checkouts' typecheck). `Object.freeze<[number, number]>([dx, dy])` is a readonly tuple on 4.8 and 4.9 alike. The compiled JavaScript is unchanged; only the source maps move.

`new Generator(height, width, { topologyId })` names the grid by id ('square' by default). `topology()` builds it lazily with core-world's `createTopology(id, width(), height())`, so it is made at the size the generator really lays out, which a subclass such as civ1-earth-generator's Earth can change from the size it was asked for. An unknown id, or a size the grid cannot wrap, throws createTopology's Error on first use.
An `options.topology` instance (0.1.6) still wins when given. The default square grid is now built through the factory, which also validates its dimensions (at least 1x1).
Needs core-world ^0.1.21 for `topologies`. The test strip topology gains the `id()` and `steps()` that ITopology now requires.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#89.

BaseGenerator called `super(height, width)`, so none of its options reached core-world-generator's `Generator`. It now passes them on, so the `topologyId` option (core-world-generator 0.1.7) chooses the grid `topology()` builds; `IOptions` gains `topologyId`. Without one the grid is square, as before, and the seeded maps are unchanged.
core-world-generator is now `^0.1.7`, and core-world (dev) `^0.1.21` for `ITopology.id()` in the tests. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#89.

log: The city area is now `topology.area(x, y, 2)` kept to the tiles whose `topology.distance` from the centre is under 2.5, instead of positions 0, 4, 20 and 24 of `getSurroundingArea(2)`. On the square grid that is the same 21 tiles in the same x-major order for every world of at least 5x5: tests/fat-cross.test.ts checks it tile for tile, in order, against the old index filter for every tile of 5x5, 5x7, 7x5, 6x6, 9x11, 40x25 and 80x50 worlds (web-renderer#88).

Below 5 tiles in either direction the old filter was already wrong: `getSurroundingArea` de-duplicates the wrapped box, so the indices no longer named the corners, and on a 1x1 world the city could not work its own tile. The new rule gives every distinct tile within reach, once each, which the test also checks for every world up to 6x6 that is narrower or shorter than 5.

chore: carry package-lock.json to 0.1.19 (missed by the version commit)

A second ITopology (civ-clone/web-renderer#93): six neighbours, all sharing an edge, x always wrapping (an east-west cylinder) and y wrapping only when asked, which needs an even height. Not wired into World yet (web-renderer#89).

distance is whole hex steps. It is computed in half-hex columns, where the axes separate, so the shortest wrap is found per axis instead of over the nine axial candidates; the tests check it against the axial formula over every candidate and against a breadth-first search over neighbour.
area returns rings outward from the centre, each walked clockwise from its corner due east, leaving out tiles past a pole that does not wrap.

A second `ITopology` for web-renderer#96 (part of web-renderer#86): diamond tiles stored in rows with every odd row shifted half a tile right, as Civ2 and Freeciv store them, so the world stays a rectangle on screen and wraps east to west. Directions are named as they look on screen; the edge directions are `ne se sw nw`. It is not wired into `World` yet (web-renderer#89).

In logical coordinates `a = (d + y) / 2`, `b = (y - d) / 2`, with `d = 2x + (y & 1)`, the grid is the square grid turned through 45°, so `distance` is `hypot(Δa, Δb)` and `area` is the same Chebyshev box in the same order as `SquareTopology.area`. Away from the seams both agree with `SquareTopology` over the same logical tiles, bit for bit.

The shortest way round is found per axis in (`d`, `y`), where wrapping east to west moves only `d` and wrapping north to south only `y`, so `distance` allocates nothing and costs about one `hypot`, as the square one does.
North to south wrapping defaults to an even height; `validate` rejects an odd height asked to wrap. Off an edge that does not wrap, `neighbour` returns `null` and `area` leaves the tiles out.

A topology made with an odd height and `wrapY` set had no consistent geometry (a distance of 0.707 between two different tiles, neighbours that were not symmetric) and only `World.topology()` calling `validate` kept that from being reachable. The constructor now calls `validate` itself, so such an object cannot exist.

The same guard StaggeredIsoTopology got in #3: an odd height asked to wrap north to south has no consistent geometry, so the constructor calls `validate` itself rather than relying on `World.topology()` to do it.

For web-renderer#88: callers that count moves (simple-ai-client's `movesBetween`, which decides whether an aircraft can still reach a city or carrier on the fuel it has left) need a measure that means the same on every grid. `distance` does not: it is the straight line on the square and staggered isometric grids but a step count on the hexagonal one.
`steps(x1, y1, x2, y2)` is the fewest neighbour-to-neighbour moves, the short way round any wrap, and allocates nothing:
SquareTopology: king's moves, `max(|dx|, |dy|)` with each axis measured the short way round as `distance` measures it.
StaggeredIsoTopology: king's moves in logical coordinates, worked out in (d, y) where the wraps separate by axis, as `distance` is: `(|Δd| + |Δy|) / 2`.
HexOddRTopology: `distance`, which is already a step count.

The tests check `steps` against a breadth-first search over `neighbour` on every topology (including worlds of one or two tiles a side), the square one against the Chebyshev distance over every way round and against `movesBetween`'s own formula for every pair of tiles on 80x50, 40x25, 10x10, 7x5 and 1x1, and the isometric one against `SquareTopology.steps` over the same logical tiles.

The workflow now installs with pnpm on Node 22 without a lock file, as the other engine repos do, and fails if the committed `.js`, `.d.ts` or `.js.map` is stale or missing. `prettier:check` now actually checks (it had no `--check`, so it printed the files and always passed).

This repo commits `tsc`'s declaration output unformatted, so the `prettier` scripts leave `.d.ts` out (`'**/!(*.d).ts'`) and the workflow has no formatting step before the stale-output check. The unused `package-lock.json` goes, since the install no longer reads it.

`Generator#topology()` returns the `topology` constructor option if one is given, otherwise a `SquareTopology(width, height)` made the first time it is asked for, and `getNeighbours`/`distanceFrom` pass it to the library functions. `topology()` is on `IGenerator` too; every implementation extends `Generator`.

`lib/getNeighbours` and `lib/distanceFrom` keep their signatures and gain an optional trailing `topology`, a square one of the given size when it is left out. `getNeighbours` maps `edgeDirections()` (direct) or `directions()` through `topology.neighbour()` and drops nulls, which a square grid never returns; `distanceFrom` is `topology.distance()` of the two tiles' coordinates.

No change on the square grid: `edgeDirections()`/`directions()` are the `n e s w` / `n ne e se s sw w nw` the literal arrays had, `neighbour()` wraps exactly as `coordsToIndex` does, and `distance()` is bit-identical to the nine-candidate formula. `tests/topology.test.ts` checks the new functions and methods against the old implementations, copied in as the oracle, for every index (and some out of range) in both modes and every pair of indices, on eleven sizes from 1x1 to 40x25, odd and even.
core-world `^0.1.19` for `ITopology` and `SquareTopology`. `SquareTopology` imports nothing from this package, so the runtime import adds no cycle.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#88.

CI now runs `ts:compile -- --force` and `prettier:format`, then fails if any compiled `.js`, `.d.ts` or `.js.map` is stale or uncommitted, as in the other repos' standard workflow (civ-clone/web-renderer#66). Rebuilt `Rules/DistributionGroups.js.map`, which 3a1989f's reformat left stale, so the new step passes.
`package-lock.json` pinned core-world 0.1.10 and none of the test tooling; CI installs with pnpm and no lock file, so nothing reads it.

movesBetween worked out the Chebyshev (king-move) distance itself, with its own wrap arithmetic. It now asks the world's topology for steps(), which core-world 0.1.20 added for exactly this: the fewest neighbour moves between two tiles, the short way round any wrap. On the square grid that is the same number for every pair of tiles; on another grid it is that grid's move count.
Not distanceFrom: that is the straight-line distance, which would change which aircraft turn for home (web-renderer#88, decision D2).

tests/movesBetween.test.ts keeps the old arithmetic as an oracle and checks every pair of tiles on nine world sizes, from 1x1 to 80x50, odd and even, across both seams. core-world's range becomes ^0.1.20 for steps().

`generateIslands` called core-world-generator's `lib/getNeighbours` with its own height and width, and `getNeighbours()` was overridden to do the same, so the islands and the terrain clusters and paths always used square neighbours whatever grid the generator was for. Both now go through `Generator#getNeighbours`, which since core-world-generator 0.1.6 asks the generator's `topology()`; the override and the library import are gone.

No change on the square grid: the square topology's edge directions are `n e s w`, the order the library returned, and its `neighbour()` wraps as `coordsToIndex` does, so every map is the same for the same seed. `tests/BaseGenerator.test.ts` pins the terrain (a SHA-1 of the map) and the number of random draws for 15 seeded maps from 10x10 to 80x50, recorded with the previous code, using rules that fill, cluster and path terrain so every neighbour and distance lookup is exercised; reversing one neighbour list or doubling the cluster distance fails them. Another test gives the generator a topology with two edge directions and checks generation asks it.
core-world-generator `^0.1.6` for `Generator#topology()`, and core-world `^0.1.19` (dev) for the `SquareTopology` the test uses.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#88.

The workflow ran `yarn install` on Node 18 and a `prettier:check` script without `--check`, which printed the formatted files and always passed. It is now the standard workflow (civ-clone/web-renderer#66): pnpm with no lock file on Node 22, `prettier --check`, `ts:compile -- --force` and `prettier:format`, then a failure if any compiled `.js`, `.d.ts` or `.js.map` is stale or uncommitted, then the tests.
`yarn.lock` and `.yarnrc.yml` are removed: nothing installs with yarn now.

log: Neighbours, edge neighbours, distance and surrounding areas were written out for a square grid in `Tile` and `Tileset`. They now go through an `ITopology` that the `World` owns, with `SquareTopology` as the only implementation, so an isometric or hexagonal grid can be added later without touching the callers (web-renderer#86, web-renderer#87).

`SquareTopology` reproduces today's results exactly: the same direction order, the same `distanceFrom` (`shortestOnAxis` and the `Math.hypot` call moved verbatim), and `area` returns `Tileset.fromSurrounding`'s x-major box. Offsets are shared frozen tuples, so `getNeighbour` allocates nothing, and the `_neighbours` cache stays. `IAdjacentTiles` and `INeighbouringTiles` remain as aliases of the square direction types, and no method signature on `Tile` changes.

The topology is transient and built lazily from the saved dimensions. `World.onHydrated` sets it to `null` so `Game.inject`'s check for transient fields left `undefined` passes without a new entry in `core-game`.
The comment said `ITopology.distance` has the history of the distance calculation; the interface has a one-line doc and the history moved with the algorithm into `SquareTopology.distance`.

Computer players now go for a space victory: once they know Computers they build the Apollo Program, research the advances a spaceship needs, build its parts in their best cities and launch it as Civilization's own computer players do, never with less than a 40% chance of arriving (closes #376).
A computer player with a spaceship in flight keeps an extra defender in its capital.
In games saved earlier, civilizations whose spaceships had ended up sharing one ship get one each again, and a part finished after a ship has launched no longer joins it.

log: chore: set up the package

A VictoryGoal has a weight and the advances it needs; goalFor picks the heaviest. ResearchForGoal researches the way to a goal's advances, found from the ruleset's Requirements rules. The space race (spaceRaceGoal, played by a SpaceRacePolicy) builds what gives a ship (BuildSpaceship), then its parts, and launches it (LaunchSpaceship). VictoryDependencies carries what these need beyond base-strategy-ai's Dependencies (civ-clone/web-renderer#376).

Review follow-ups: the probe's stand-ins are made with Object.create rather than new, so it no longer takes ids from each advance's class (a game would otherwise number its advances differently once the probe had run), and its cache is keyed on both registries.
Merge pull request #1 from civ-clone/feat/space-race

Before 0.1.3 the Apollo Program gave every player's ship the same layout, so each player's parts went into everyone's ship. A Start rule now gives each ship still being built that shares its layout a layout of its own, with the parts its player's cities built; a ship in flight keeps what it launched with (civ-clone/web-renderer#376).

Parts still in production when a ship launched were added to it in flight, changing its flight time and chance of success after launch. They're now left behind, as a ship can't change in flight (civ-clone/web-renderer#376).

Review follow-ups (civ-clone/web-renderer#376): at a turn's start, a player whose ship is in flight stops building parts, which would only be left behind; a ship still being built that shares its layout with any other ship, launched or not, gets its own; and a player who came into the game after the Apollo Program was built (a civilization coming back, #178) gets a ship.
Merge pull request #3 from civ-clone/fix/own-layouts
civ1-spaceship#2 moves the arrival check from Rules/Turn/start to Rules/Turn/end and gives the Apollo Program's ships to every player (civ-clone/web-renderer#177).

civ1-science's repeatable Future Technology (civ-clone/web-renderer#458) is on offer to a player who knows nearly everything, which every ChooseResearch test's player does, so it crowded out the advances each test is about (civ-clone/web-renderer#66).

Once a player knows Computers, or has a ship with parts on it, it plays for space (base-strategy-victory): it researches Space Flight, Plastics and Robotics, builds the Apollo Program in its most productive city, then a ship in balanced steps in its most productive third of cities, and launches by v474.05's rules: never under a 40% chance; when the ship is complete, better than 75%, outranked, or a rival's ship would arrive no sooner; not while no rival knows Space Flight. Ours on top: a complete ship, or one that would otherwise arrive within 10 years of the final year, launches. A capital keeps a defender more while its ship is in flight (civ-clone/web-renderer#376).

Review follow-ups: a Propulsion waits for its Fuel, not the frame, so it no longer asks for a Structural, and none is wanted once the frame has no room; a city still wanting defenders builds those before the Apollo Program or parts; and science doesn't stop while a player playing for space lacks an advance its ship needs (civ-clone/web-renderer#376).

`FutureTechnology` is a repeatable advance (core-science), registered with the others. Its requirement is every non-repeatable advance in the game's advance registry, so `requirements` now takes the registry. Each one completed counts towards the cost of the next, as `DiscoveredTechnologyCount` does in v474.05. Capturing a city never takes one (civ-clone/web-renderer#128).
`stealableAdvances` leaves out advances marked `repeatable` (core-science), so Future Technology can't be stolen (civ-clone/web-renderer#128).

An `Advance` with `static repeatable = true` stays in `available()` once it's known, and completing or adding it again appends another instance to `complete()`, so the number held is the count of its instances. Nothing new is saved. Packages that hand advances between players are expected to leave repeatable ones out (civ-clone/web-renderer#128).

log: For civ-clone/web-renderer#284: the greedy step broke ties with a random comparator, which isn't a fair shuffle. With eight tied neighbours the first listed (North) was taken about 53% of the time. The scored steps are now shuffled with the game's RNG (Fisher–Yates, `lib/shuffle`) and sorted by score alone (stable). Among tied steps, the one straight on from the unit's last step comes first, which keeps a wandering unit heading somewhere: with a plain fair pick the arena read power −2.0, powerUnits −2.4 and shields −2.0 (t) on seeds 1–40 (flat on 41–80); with the heading no metric reaches |t| ≥ 2 on either set.

invasions go only for the focus's cities, and invaders gather in port until their attack is `MUSTER` (2) × the defence on the target's landmass (with `AttackConfidence`), or they've waited `MUSTER_WAIT` (15) turns. `Earth` now builds the map for the size it's asked for, the sizes New Game calls Normal, Large and Huge. Any other size gets the original 80 x 50 map, and `width()` / `height()` report the size actually generated.

The larger maps are Civilization's own map scaled up, so the continents keep their shape and terrain, with the coasts refined from real coastlines and some islands the original leaves out (Sri Lanka, New Zealand, Ireland, Sicily...). Britain stays apart from the continent at every size.
Each map lives in `Maps/` with its own start tiles, and `EarthStartTile` now holds one per size, so `startTileForMap()` picks the one for the `World` it's given.

`python3 generate.py` rebuilds `Maps/Earth104x65.ts` and `Maps/Earth128x80.ts` from `Maps/Earth80x50.ts` and Natural Earth's public-domain land polygons; the README has the download and how it works. The download, its caches and the preview it draws are ignored.

civ1TerrainPolicy finds the cheapest way between each city and its two nearest neighbours within ten squares (civ-clone/web-renderer#384), within an ellipse around the pair, preferring straight lines between equal costs, and offers a Road on each tile of it (worth 1), then a Railroad once Railroad is known. The way is cached per player per turn, and its tiles join the policy's job tiles.
Once Railroad is known, a Road's value includes what the Railroad it allows would add, so a Road goes down on a River where the Road alone adds nothing (civ-clone/web-renderer#385).

Polluted tiles get a cleanPollution job, valued by the yields the pollution costs (weighted as other jobs), plus 1, plus a quarter for each other polluted tile the player has, times the leader's PollutionConcern (base-leader-personality 0.1.1; civ-clone/web-renderer#366).

The policy now wants a terrain worker for every six cities rather than eight: in the arena, with routes to build, one for every six gave more linked cities on both seed sets and nothing worse; one for every four founded fewer cities (civ-clone/web-renderer#234).

localChanges: Computer players' Settlers, and your Automated Settlers, now build Roads, and later Railroads, along the way between neighbouring cities (closes #384).
Once you know Railroad, they also build a Road where only the Railroad on it would pay, such as on a River (closes #385).
They clean up pollution, and computer players whose leaders mind it more get to it sooner (closes #366).
Computer players keep one Settlers improving the land for every six cities, up from one for every eight (closes #234).
chore: lock the engine packages that teach Settlers to clear terrain and carry water

log: `TerrainJobValue.improvement` widens to a string and gains an optional `action` (the `ActionLookup` name the worker needs), so a ruleset can offer jobs that aren't improvements, such as clearing a Swamp (civ-clone/web-renderer#353, #386). The four existing improvements keep their actions, so an existing policy runs unchanged.

`TerrainPolicy.tiles` optionally names the tiles a worker may be sent to; by default the player's cities' tiles, as before. A job that carries water to a dry tile can lie outside every city radius (civ-clone/web-renderer#426).

`jobCircumstances` fingerprints which terrain and which improvements are on a tile and its neighbours rather than counting improvements, so one improvement replacing another, or a terrain change, forgets a remembered undoable job at once (civ-clone/web-renderer#255).
Play is unchanged for an existing policy: an arena run of the pinned simple-ai-client on this package against itself gave a delta of exactly 0.
`civ1TerrainPolicy`:
Food is weighted by the city's food surplus (0 or less, 1, 2, 3, more) rather than a single "at most 1" step, and irrigation counts a quarter more than its food alone (civ-clone/web-renderer#383).

`clearSwamp` and `clearJungle` (to Grassland) on a worked tile with no feature; `clearForest` (to Plains) with no feature where the Plains could then be irrigated, with that irrigation counted in, on a worked tile or one that carries water on (civ-clone/web-renderer#353, #386). Planting Forest was tried and dropped: it cost more than it gave in the arena.

A tile that could carry water (irrigable or a Forest with water beside it, not Hills) to a cardinal neighbour worth irrigating but dry is worth half of that irrigation too; `tiles()` adds such tiles outside the city radii. A dry tile water could reach isn't mined first when irrigating it would be worth more, and irrigation that is a neighbour's only water isn't mined until the neighbour is irrigated (civ-clone/web-renderer#426).

Tests cover the weights, each conversion and its conditions, and two maps run job by job until none is left: the one from #426 (its Desert Oasis is irrigated) and one where only a Forest outside the city radius can carry the water. Needs base-strategy-terrain-work 0.1.2.

Arena (80 games, 300 turns, two seed sets): score, population and cities unchanged; minedTiles -0.3 and -0.6 (t -1.5, -3.0). Dom chose to ship it for the jobs it gives Automated Settlers; details on civ-clone/web-renderer#353.

localChanges: Computer players' Settlers, and your Automated Settlers, now irrigate first around cities that are short of food (closes #383).
They also clear Swamp and Jungle on squares a city works, and clear Forest where the Plains left behind can then be irrigated (closes #353, closes #386).
When a square worth irrigating has no water next to it, they bring the water to it first, for example by clearing a Forest beside the sea and irrigating the Plains (closes #426).
chore: lock the engine packages that announce cities growing, shrinking and starving

log: CityGrowth.grow()/shrink() only process the Grow/Shrink rules and nothing emitted, so a renderer listening for these events never heard them (civ-clone/web-renderer#400).
civ1-city:city/grow/emit, last of the Grow rules.
civ1-city:city/shrink/emit, while size > 0; a city shrunk to nothing is destroyed instead, which emits city:destroyed.
civ1-city:city/food-exhausted/emit, before the shrink, so famine is known before the shrinking (or destruction) it causes.
getRules for grow, shrink and food-exhausted take an Engine (last, defaulting to the instance); registerRules passes game.engine.
Uses core-city-growth's new grow/shrink cause (civ-clone/core-city-growth feat/growth-cause), so a listener can tell why a city's size changed (civ-clone/web-renderer#400):
famine shrinks with FoodExhausted (the rule type);
a capture shrinks with Captured;
a lost defence shrinks with the Attack that won.
The emit rules send the cause as the event's second argument, `null` when nothing was given.
chore: require core-city-growth 0.1.6, which passes a grow/shrink cause
A city held at 10 without an Aqueduct shrinks with Aqueduct as the cause (core-city-growth feat/growth-cause), so a listener can tell it from other losses (civ-clone/web-renderer#400).
chore: require core-city-growth 0.1.6, which passes a grow/shrink cause
Passes a cause to CityGrowth#shrink (core-city-growth feat/growth-cause), so a listener can tell Settlers built and a nuclear strike from other losses (civ-clone/web-renderer#400).
chore: require core-city-growth 0.1.6, which passes a grow/shrink cause

As City#capture does: what a ruleset passes is up to it (the Settlers built, the attack lost, the rule type that starved the city), so a Grow or Shrink rule, and a listener the ruleset tells, can react to why the size changed (civ-clone/web-renderer#400). Nothing passed is null.
Grow and Shrink are now Rule<[CityGrowth, unknown], void>.

localChanges: The Reveal Map cheat no longer sends every newly revealed square a second time, under a name the map never read (closes #342).
A city of yours that is captured or destroyed now leaves a notice beside End Turn, showing your city, instead of a window that was easy to miss among the other civilizations' moves (closes #420).
Famine in one of your cities is now announced, and a city's size changes on the map and in its screen as soon as it grows or shrinks (closes #400).
chore: lock the engine package that sends each city's pollution

log: A smokestacks AdditionalData on City: the city's smokestack points over 20 (lib/smokestacks), never below 0, so a renderer can draw Civ1's pollution indicator without knowing the rule (civ-clone/web-renderer#402).
lib/smokestacks is now lib/pollution (export pollution), and the AdditionalData on City is keyed pollution, so the shared concept isn't named after how Civ1 draws it (civ-clone/web-renderer#402).

localChanges: A city at risk of polluting the land around it now shows a smokestack for each point of risk, in a row below its Luxuries, Gold and Research. Hover over them for the amount (#402).
In a large game, moving a unit, changing what a city builds or buying it now sends the map a few kilobytes instead of your whole civilization again, so each shows several times sooner (closes #411).

A turn in a large game now sends the map about a third less data, because a city or a notice no longer carries every square it touches in full, only the squares that actually changed. Changing which squares a city works, a revolution's new yields, and a rival entering a hut now redraw the squares they alter straight away (closes #138). A Settlers that founded a city is no longer left drawn on the square afterwards.

Computer players take their turns about a quarter quicker late in the game: they no longer list a square's surroundings, flood a continent, size up their units or work out a city's output more than once a turn (closes #316, closes #317, closes #408). Sending a unit somewhere with GoTo starts sooner, because the route is planned once rather than twice (closes #307), and working out what a city can build checks far fewer rules (closes #185).

log: Moved out of simple-ai-client (civ-clone/web-renderer#198, #200) unchanged apart from imports: Dependencies (with dependenciesFor), Knowledge (with MartialLawPolicy), Memory (with UncalmedReason), MemoryRegistry, actionLookup, the survey (its StrategyNote key stays 'simple-ai-client:survey' so saved games resume), the unit turn context, orders, reachable, AIStrategy, isUnitAction, unitTurnContextFor, and the Mission type with nearest and pursue. The library-unit imports are now the base-unit-type-* / base-unit-action-* classes they re-export.

New: UnitOrder (a PlayerAction<Unit> for a standing order, never a mandatory action), OrderStrategy with findStrategy and isOrderStrategy, followPath (a synchronous mover that only moves, honours canReturnAfter, and reports arrived / blocked / threatened / out-of-moves) and enemyAdjacent (the test that wakes a sleeping unit).

`pursue` flooded the unit's whole continent or sea (`reachableTiles`) for every unit given a mission, for each mission it was offered: about 90 floods a computer turn on web-renderer's turn-287 save, 6% of the turn (civ-clone/web-renderer#316). `reachableTiles` takes the turn now: given it, what it finds from a tile the unit could move on to is kept for the turn and shared by every tile of that continent or sea, by kind (land or sea), so callers must only ask it `has`. From anywhere else, such as a land unit aboard a ship, it's found afresh, as it isn't one continent. Without the turn, nothing changes. `pursue` passes the turn.

No rule turns land into sea or sea into land, so the sets are the ones a fresh flood finds; they're dropped each turn all the same. web-renderer's conformance run is unchanged, checksums and ids alike.

New rules on core-city's `TileWorked` and `TileReleased`, which `WorkedTileRegistry` processes for every tile a city starts or stops working, emit `city:tile-worked` and `city:tile-released` with the city and the tile, as `city:created` and the rest are emitted. A client sends the tile, whose `workedBy` changed, from them (civ-clone/web-renderer#138). Needs core-city 0.1.22.

Each rule names its improvement, and the one that stops a city building a second of the same names CityImprovement, so units, wonders and spaceship parts no longer check it. The criteria are unchanged and still decide.
Needs the core-city-build release that lets Build take items.
civ-clone/web-renderer#185
Each rule names its part (or Part, for the two that apply to every part), so CityBuild checks a part against its own rules rather than all ~100. The criteria are unchanged and still decide.
Needs the core-city-build release that lets Build take items.
civ-clone/web-renderer#185
Each rule names its unit (or Naval, for the coastal one), so CityBuild checks a unit against its own two or three rules rather than all ~100. The criteria are unchanged and still decide.
Needs the core-city-build release that lets Build take items.
civ-clone/web-renderer#185

The goto criterion searches for a route to decide whether GoTo is on offer, and GoTo#perform then searched for the same route again. The criterion now keeps the route it found, and the effect hands it to the GoTo through a PlannedPathFinderRegistry (lib/): its path finder returns that route for the first search for the same unit, start and end, and searches as before for anything else. base-unit-action-goto is unchanged.

Every action's criteria are validated before any effect runs, so the route is kept with the unit, from and to it was found for, and the effect only uses one that matches. Performed from anywhere other than where it was offered, the GoTo searches again, as before.

On the turn-287 save, 157 GoTos by the human player's land units to their furthest city on the same land mass take 157 searches instead of 314, and every unit ends on the same tile (civ-clone/web-renderer#307).

The route a GoTo was offered with is dropped as soon as a unit moves, is created, destroyed or changes hands, or a city is created, destroyed or captured, anywhere. A GoTo performed after that searches again, so it never follows a route through a tile that has since been occupied. A GoTo performed straight after it was offered still costs one search (civ-clone/web-renderer#307).

Each rule names its wonder (or Wonder, for the one-per-game rule, and Nuclear for the Manhattan Project one), so CityBuild checks a wonder against its own rules rather than all ~100. The criteria are unchanged and still decide.
Needs the core-city-build release that lets Build take items.
civ-clone/web-renderer#185

`WorkedTileRegistry` processes `TileWorked` (`[City, Tile]`) after each tile it registers, and `TileReleased` after each one it unregisters. `unregister` is overridden, so `unregisterByTile` is covered, and a worked tile that isn't registered releases nothing. Every way a tile comes to be worked or released goes through the registry (founding, growth, shrinking, `changeWorkedTile`, `reassignWorkers`, an enemy unit in the way, a city destroyed), so a client can follow `workedBy` from these without the callers changing (civ-clone/web-renderer#138).
Both are notifications. Unlike `TileReassigned`, nothing processing them should change which tiles are worked.

Loading a save processes nothing. `hydrate` restores membership through `register`, but makes each `WorkedTile` with `Object.create`, which never calls the constructor. `WorkedTile` keeps a `WeakSet` of the ones it constructed, and `isRestored` answers for the rest. A restored tile still processes `TileReleased` when it's later unregistered.
Once per tile, not once per call: `assignWorkers` registers one tile per call anyway, and the only many-tile `register` is the load.

`WorkedTileRegistry` skipped `TileWorked` for a tile restored from a save for the object's whole lifetime, so registering it, unregistering it and registering it again processed only `TileReleased`. The restoration mark is now consumed by the first registration, which is the one loading a game performs. Registering the same object again later is an ordinary change and processes `TileWorked`.

CityBuild#available() checked every available item against every Build rule (~100 rules x ~76 items = ~7,750 validate calls per city, nearly all of them for a different item). A criterion is an opaque function, so the only way to skip them is for the rule to say what it is about.

Build now takes items (the classes themselves, so Warrior or Wonder) among its constructor values. A rule that declares some is only checked for those items and anything extending them (Build#mayApplyTo); a rule that declares none is checked for every item, as before. The criterion still runs and still decides for the items the rule is checked for, so a declaration only narrows it and an undeclared ruleset behaves exactly as it did.

buildRulesFor() keeps the rules for each item against the array RuleRegistry#get hands back, which is a new array whenever a rule is registered, unregistered, enabled or disabled, so nothing needs invalidating.
civ-clone/web-renderer#185

The survey asks `shouldBuildCity` about every tile the player knows, every turn (23k calls on the turn-287 save), and each call built a radius-2 `Tileset` to score and, for a site that scored well enough, a radius-4 one to look for cities in. Building them was over half of the survey (civ-clone/web-renderer#317). `surroundingArea` lists a tile's surroundings once, as `Tile#getSurroundingArea` does (same tiles, same order, each once on a map small enough to wrap), since the map's shape doesn't change. Each tile's score as part of a site's surroundings is kept with the yields list it was worked out from, and worked out again once `Tile#yields` hands back a new one (after `clearYieldCache`), so every candidate site within two tiles of it reuses it.

`buildItemInCity` flooded the city's continent once or twice for every city, every decision. `continentOf` finds each continent once a turn and shares the set between its tiles (civ-clone/web-renderer#316); callers only ask it `has`. No rule turns land into sea or sea into land, but the cache is dropped each turn all the same. From a sea tile it isn't kept, as that isn't one continent.
Same decisions: web-renderer's conformance run is unchanged, checksums and ids alike.

civ1-treasury's Spend rule for units now asks the rules whether the city is in civil disorder. Registered without a registry, it asked the game-wide one, where an earlier test file's civil disorder rules, bound to that file's city growths, threw "Wrong number of CityGrowths returned" for this suite's cities: 10 tests failed in CI on master after a fresh install. The suite's own registry holds its own civil disorder rules.

The Explorer check asked for the city's continent before `reachableLandToExplore` could answer 0 for an empty list of tiles to explore, so the first city on a continent each turn flooded it for nothing when no Settler check needed it either (a size-one city, say). The list is checked first now, and the continent is only looked up with something to explore.

civ-clone/web-renderer#307 proposed caching stepCost per (from, to) for the life of a search. There is nothing for it to save: generate() costs a tile's neighbours only when it expands the tile, and the done set expands each tile once, so every step is costed exactly once per search. On the turn-287 save, the second turn after load costs 99,879 steps in 85 searches with no repeat inside any search. The test pins that, and stepCost's comment says why there is no cache.

localChanges: A unit now moves on the map the moment you press the key, instead of after the game has confirmed the move, and keys you type while a move is being confirmed are kept and played in order rather than lost. A move the game refuses, such as into a rival's zone of control, snaps the unit back (closes #326).
test: patchRefs no longer mistakes the CityBuild player action for a build carrying available (#410)

A loaded game is ready a little sooner, and a new game starts a little quicker too. The game used to send the page everything about your civilization twice when a turn began for the first time, and the page built it twice over; now it is sent and built once (closes #333).
If one square of the map can't be drawn, the rest of the map still draws, and its cities, units and names stay lined up with the land (#32).
Clicking a city with a polluted square nearby opens its city screen again, instead of doing nothing (#32).
The map no longer slips out of line with its cities, units and city names when it moves over polluted squares, such as when you open a city.
test: check a cleaned square's Food without clearing its yield cache first
fix: Create Unit refuses a fractional or negative square instead of rounding it to another
chore: lock the engine packages that let Nuclear units detonate and Settlers clean up pollution

log: A worker cleans the pollution off its tile over the turns the ruleset's MovementCost gives it; finishing processes core-tile-improvement's Removed rules for each Pollution there (civ-clone/web-renderer#32). Registered with registerDelayedAction so a unit part-way through survives a save.

The action processes Moved, then the ruleset's Detonated rules, then destroys the weapon if they haven't (civ-clone/web-renderer#129). SneakNuclearAttack carries the enemy whose peace treaty it breaks, as SneakAttack does.

With Moved first, a ruleset's contact rule met the units about to be destroyed: in civ1-diplomacy that opened a negotiation with a civilization the detonation then wiped out, and the client's patches waited on the answer (found checking civ-clone/web-renderer#129 in the browser).
Each turn, as v474.05 does (CityWorker.cs ~L188-200, L705-768, L3710-3751), for every city (the AI's too, as decided on civ-clone/web-renderer#32):

lib/smokestacks: floor(shields / divisor) + floor(size * level / 4) - 20, where shields are after the Factory/plant bonuses and before unit support, the divisor is the largest PollutionDivisor rule (Hydro or Nuclear Plant 2, Recycling Center 3, else 1) and the level is the polluting advances known (Industrialization, Automobile, Mass Production, Plastics), 0 with Mass Transit.

civ1-city-improvement:city/process-yield/pollution: when 2 * points beats a roll of 0 .. 255 - advances known * difficulty / 2, a random square around the city is polluted, unless it's water, a city or already polluted; emits city:polluted.
PollutionDivisor: a new rule type, so civ1-wonder can add Hoover Dam.
The commented-out Pollution yield modifiers are gone: this replaces them.
test: add simple-world-generator as a devDependency, for the pollution test's FillGenerator
As for a built one, so every player who knows the tile sees its yields change when pollution is cleaned up (civ-clone/web-renderer#32).

A Nuclear unit no longer gets Attack/SneakAttack. It gets NuclearAttack (or SneakNuclearAttack when the target's owner is at peace) against a neighbouring tile holding another player's unit or city, never empty land.
The Detonated rules follow v474.05 (Segment_29f3.cs F0_29f3_0d4d/0ec3):
emit unit:nuclear-detonation before anything changes;
destroy every unit on the target and its 8 neighbours, whoever owns it, except in a city with SDI Defense (emits city:sdi-protected);
halve every city in the area (size -= floor(size / 2)), SDI or not;
pollute each land, non-city tile in the area with a 2 in 3 chance.
civ-clone/web-renderer#129
civ1-unit:unit/action/clean-pollution: a Worker on a polluted square can CleanPollution, which takes 4 turns in Civ1 terms on any terrain (Table 3-2; v474.05 CheckPlayerTurn.cs ~L1050).
Fallout builds the Pollution by constructing it (which processes Built) rather than processing Built a second time, and skips squares already polluted, as v474.05's AddPollutionToCell does.
civ-clone/web-renderer#32, civ-clone/web-renderer#129

Destroying a transport lost at sea destroys its cargo through the Destroyed rules, and the loop over the tile's units then processed that cargo a second time, duplicating unit:destroyed. Skip units already destroyed.
A PollutionDivisor of 2 in its owner's cities on its continent, as a Hydro Plant gives (v474.05 CityWorker.cs ~L741-753, civ-clone/web-renderer#32).
A polluted tile yields half its food, shields and trade, rounded up, after everything else (v474.05 CityWorker.cs ~L4138): a Low priority YieldModifier pushing the difference.
Removed (core-tile-improvement 0.1.6): unregister the improvement, clear the tile's yield cache, emit tile-improvement:removed.
civ-clone/web-renderer#32
For an improvement taken off a tile other than by pillaging, such as pollution cleaned up by Settlers (civ-clone/web-renderer#32).
Re-exported from the new base-unit-action-nuclear-attack package, for Civ1's nuclear detonation (civ-clone/web-renderer#129).
Re-exported from the new base-unit-action-clean-pollution package (civ-clone/web-renderer#32).

localChanges: Cities with heavy industry, or large populations once Industrialization, the Automobile, Mass Production and Plastics are known, now pollute the squares around them, and you're told "Pollution near Beijing." A Hydro Plant, Nuclear Plant or Hoover Dam halves a city's pollution from industry, a Recycling Center cuts it to a third, and Mass Transit stops its people polluting (closes #32).
A polluted square yields half its food, shields and trade. Settlers clean it up in 4 turns with the new Clean up pollution order (p).
Nuclear fallout is the same pollution, so it now halves a square's yields too and can be cleaned up.
With cheats on, the game menu's Create Unit places any kind of unit for you or another civilization on a chosen square. Click the map while it's open to pick the square.

A Nuclear unit no longer fights like an ordinary attacker. It detonates when it attacks a rival unit or moves into a rival city, destroying every unit in the 3×3 area (yours too), halving each city there and leaving fallout on the land around it. Other civilizations are told when nuclear weapons are used (closes #129).
A city with SDI Defense keeps its units safe from a nuclear attack, though it is still halved.

It ends the journey one tile short with the unit awake and processes the new Halted rule with the destination, so a client can offer the choice (civ-clone/web-renderer#357).
GoTo.perform only marks the unit GoTo-busy while its journey is still under way: a journey ended on the first leg (blocked, arrived or halted) used to leave the unit awake but still showing GoTo.

Covers civ-clone/web-renderer#281: Forest+Game clears to Plains+Horse, Swamp+Oil / Jungle+Gems / Plains+Horse plant to Forest+Game, and Grassland's Shield or no special leaves none. Needs base-unit-action-clear-forest and base-unit-action-plant-forest published with the fix.

JsBachsCathedral: only the owner's cities on its own continent.

Tests cover base 12 with the Library/University stand-ins (now Low, as the real rules are) registered before and after this package's.

localChanges: Isaac Newton's College now raises the science from every Library and University you own, until anyone discovers Nuclear Fission.
Hoover Dam now powers every city you have on its continent that has a Factory, as if each had its own power plant (closes #115).
With Michelangelo's Chapel, a Cathedral now makes six unhappy citizens content rather than eight, and J.S. Bach's Cathedral only calms your cities on its own continent, as in Civ1 (closes #236).
chore: lock the engine packages that give defenders Civ1's terrain, City Walls and fortified bonuses

log: The defender is the unit on the tile with the highest defence against this attacker, and the roll uses both units' `strength()`, so rules for terrain, City Walls and fortification apply in battle (civ-clone/web-renderer#31). With no `Strength` rules it fights as before. Needs core-unit 0.1.27.

A `Strength` rule (core-unit 0.1.27) gives a defender v474.05's bonuses for one battle: its terrain's multiplier (Forest, Jungle, River, Swamp ×1.5, Hills ×2, Mountains ×3), then the first of City Walls (×3, not against Artillery or a Bomber) or fortified (×1.5). A ship gets only City Walls, in a city; an aircraft gets nothing. Fortified leaves the unit's own `Defence` yield, where it added ×2, and is only counted in battle. For civ-clone/web-renderer#31.

v474.05's City Walls branch (`Segment_29f3.cs` `F0_29f3_000e`) sets the defence to terrain × defence × 12/4 for any defender but an aircraft, replacing a ship's flat value, so a Sail in a walled city on Hills defends at 6. The comment said ships get no terrain bonus without that exception; the test now says why it expects 6.

`Strength` (attacker, defender, attack, defence) changes the strengths two units fight at, for bonuses that aren't part of either unit's own `attack()` or `defence()`: terrain, City Walls, a fortified defender. `strength()` starts from those and processes the rules; with none it gives today's numbers. For civ-clone/web-renderer#31.

`scoreUnitMove` compares the attacker's and the defender's `strength()` (core-unit 0.1.27) instead of their own `attack()` and `defence()`, against the unit that would defend, so the AI sees terrain, City Walls and a fortified defender before it attacks (civ-clone/web-renderer#31). The scoring weights are unchanged. The tests register civ1-unit's `Strength` rules.

The test compared two scores, which didn't show where an attack stops paying. A Warrior (1) against a Warrior earns the even-odds and 2/3-odds terms; behind City Walls the defender fights at 3 and the attack scores 0. Fails on the old scoring (96).

localChanges: City Walls now triple the strength of a city's defenders, except against Artillery and Bombers (#31).
A defender on Hills fights at double strength and on Mountains at triple, and Forest, Jungle, Swamp and River add half again.
A fortified unit now defends at one and a half times its strength, as in Civ1, rather than double. Behind City Walls, fortifying adds nothing more.
Ships get no help from terrain at sea or in an unwalled city. In port behind City Walls, they get the walls and the city's terrain. Aircraft get neither.
Computer players now weigh terrain, City Walls and fortified defenders before they attack.
chore: lock the engine packages that let the Great Wall and the United Nations keep other leaders peaceful

log: The `DemandTribute` step after the handover isn't offered to a player `Pacified` towards the other (library-diplomacy), as Civ1's Great Wall and United Nations make every other leader towards their owner (civ-clone/web-renderer#30). In v474.05 the tribute demand needs the leader to be hostile, which either wonder rules out (`MeetWithKing.cs` ~L359, ~L0487).

Every other player is `Pacified` towards the owner of the Great Wall (until anyone discovers Gunpowder) or of the United Nations, so in a negotiation they make no demands of it, don't turn down its peace and end by offering it peace, and computer players don't break a peace with it (civ-clone/web-renderer#30).

v474.05 clears the leader's hostility in the human's parley for either wonder (`MeetWithKing.cs` ~L359), and keeps computer players who meet from going to war with the Great Wall's owner (`Segment_2517.cs` `F0_2517_0737`). Both act in every negotiation here, since computer players meet through the same one.
The Pyramids (civ-clone/web-renderer#33), Darwin's Voyage and the Apollo Program (civ1-spaceship) already have their effects.

`Pacified` (`Rule<[Player, Player], boolean>`) says whether a player is pacified towards another: it makes no demands of it and doesn't turn down its peace when they negotiate, and doesn't break a peace with it. `isPacified` is true if any match is. Civ1's Great Wall and United Nations supply it (civ-clone/civ1-wonder), the negotiation steps (civ-clone/civ1-diplomacy) and the AI (civ-clone/simple-ai-client) read it, for civ-clone/web-renderer#30.

`shouldBeHostile` is `shouldAttack` unless the player is `Pacified` towards the other (library-diplomacy), which Civ1's Great Wall and United Nations make every other leader towards their owner (civ-clone/web-renderer#30). Negotiation uses it in place of `shouldAttack`, so a pacified AI accepts the owner's peace, offers it peace and takes its knowledge however strong it is; so do sneak attacks, sneak captures and sneak thefts, so it never breaks a peace with the owner.

localChanges: While you own the Great Wall (until anyone discovers Gunpowder) or the United Nations, other leaders make no demands of you in a parley and always end by offering you a peace treaty, as in Civ1 (#30, #115).
Computer players won't break a peace treaty with the owner of either wonder, and accept its offers of peace however strong they are.
chore: lock the engine packages that weigh computer players' units against their cities' other needs

log: A Militaristic leader weighs military units 4/3 and a Civilized one 2/3, (3 - Ideology) / 3, mirroring v474.05's improvement weighting. Settlers, Diplomats and Caravans aren't scaled. v474.05 itself scales only improvements, but its scores sit close together; in simple-ai-client's ranking a unit a player needs outscores an improvement it doesn't by more than 4/3, so the lean only acted on about 8 of 1,900 choices until units leant too (civ-clone/web-renderer#378).
core-unit moves from devDependencies to dependencies, and base-unit-type-worker and base-unit-type-diplomatic are added, for the unit classes the rule tells apart.

buildItemInCity keeps one hard rule, a city's own missing defender (wantsUnit). Every other unit quota (explorers, Settlers, attackers, a defender for an undefended city) becomes a score in BuildPriority's scale: policy.needs times how far the player is short of what it wants. Those join the improvements and Wonders ranked by BuildPriority in one ranking (rankWithUnits), each times the leader's BuildWeight, so a leader's lean acts on every choice rather than on a random pick that ran about once in 900 choices (civ-clone/web-renderer#378).

policy.needs: explorer 6 (not weighed by the leader: weighing it cost a seventh of the land explored), settlers 4, attacker 4, reinforcement 3, army 0.09 (an attacker when the player wants no more, just under an everyday improvement), fortification 2 (caps Barracks and City Walls, which civ1-city-improvement scores 100 under threat for cities on Auto), wonder 3 (added to the ruleset's score for the Wonders the AI's own gates allow).
The leader-weighted random pick is gone; nothing in production draws from the random number generator.
The fallback, for a city that needs nothing it can finish soon, now puts units it can support before Barracks and City Walls.

Arena, 80 games x 150 turns against fabfaaf: score +8.2 (t 5.0, mostly Wonders: started 1.5 vs 0.5), cities +0.14 (t 0.7), units lost -3.7 (t -3.6), land explored -11% (t -3.2). With civ1-civilization weighing military units by Ideology, the leader's weighting changes 13% of Civilized leaders' choices (away from attackers) and 5% of Militaristic ones (towards them).

The cap on what Barracks and City Walls score in a city under threat was applied to the score after `BuildWeight`, so every leader's capped at the same 2 and the lean was lost (Copilot, #41). It now caps at `fortification × weight`, i.e. `min(raw, fortification) × weight`.

Weighed, a cap of 2 let a Civilized leader's Barracks (8/3) beat its defenders (3 × 2/3), which cost power (t −2.0), advances (t −2.1) and land explored (t −2.8) against 56e7a63 in 80 arena games. At 1.5 (Civilized 2, Militaristic 1) nothing moves at |t| ≥ 2 against 56e7a63.

The cap test pitted Barracks against a reinforcement, whose score depends on whether civ1-civilization weighs military units (civ-clone/civ1-civilization#2), so it failed on CI, which resolves civ1-civilization from master. An explorer scores the same either way.
The module and `ProductionPolicy` summaries claimed every candidate is weighed by `BuildWeight` and limited by `buildTurns` (Copilot, #41).

localChanges: Computer players now choose what to build from one list of needs, units, improvements and Wonders together, and their leaders' personalities show in it: Militaristic leaders such as Genghis Khan build more fighting units, and Civilized ones such as Abraham Lincoln put more into their cities (#378).
Computer players start Wonders about three times as often.
test: a city on Auto stays on Auto through a save and load, and the conformance note says why its numbers moved
chore: lock the engine packages that put a city's production on Auto

log: `civ1-city:city/building-complete/auto` and `civ1-city:city/building-cancelled/auto` start what a city on Auto needs most (`core-city-build`'s `rankBuildItems` over `BuildPriority`) when its build is complete or can no longer be built. `lib/autoBuild` limits the choice to improvements and Wonders, never units. `civ1-city:city/captured/stop-auto` takes a captured city off Auto. Needs core-city-build 0.1.13 (civ-clone/web-renderer#194).

`civ1-city:player/turn-start/auto-build` runs `lib/autoBuild` for each of the player's cities at the start of its turn, after production. Until now a city only chose on `BuildingComplete` / `BuildingCancelled`, so a city put on Auto before its player knew any improvement worth building sat on nothing for good (civ-clone/web-renderer#194).

The filter only left out units, so anything else a city can build, such as a spaceship part, could be chosen once a `BuildPriority` scored it. Allow `CityImprovement` (Wonders included) instead. Spaceship parts are left to a space race strategy (civ-clone/web-renderer#376).
The test's `BuildPriority` and `Build` callbacks now take `IBuildable`, so it type-checks under ts-mocha.

`Rules/City/build-priority.ts` registers a `BuildPriority` for each Civ1 improvement from the city's yields and size: a Granary for a starving city (and a little for one of size 3+ with 1 Food or less to spare), an Aqueduct near size 10 (sooner with Food to spare), a Temple, Colosseum and Cathedral for unhappy citizens, a Marketplace and Bank for gold and luxuries, a Library and University for science, a Courthouse for corruption, a Factory for shields and the plants only beside a Factory. The everyday improvements (Granary, Temple, Marketplace, Library, Courthouse, Bank, University) score at least 0.1, so a city on Auto always has one to build. Each is weighed against its upkeep, as a share of the city's gold. Barracks and City Walls score only while a unit or city of a player the owner isn't at peace with is within 5 tiles, and then above everything else: Civ1 has no declared war, so having met isn't enough. `Rules/City/cost.ts` exports its upkeep tables and an `upkeep()` helper for this, with no change to the costs. Needs core-city-build 0.1.13 (civ-clone/web-renderer#194).

`Corruption` yields are negative, so the total was never 2 or more and a Courthouse only ever got the everyday floor. Negate the total, and build the test's yields the way `civ1-city` does (a positive amount, whose `value()` is negative), which the old test had backwards.

`Rules/City/build-priority.ts` gives a Wonder a `BuildPriority` of 1.5 in a city making 5 shields or more, when it isn't obsolete, would do something for its player (the Lighthouse and Magellan's only with ships; never the Manhattan Project), and none of the player's other cities is building it. Needs core-city-build 0.1.13 (civ-clone/web-renderer#194).

`CityBuild` gains `auto()` / `setAuto()` (saved as `_auto`; a build restored from an older save reads as not on Auto). `BuildPriority` rules score `(cityBuild, item, yields)`, with the city's yields worked out once per ranking; `lib/rankBuildItems` adds the matches, weighs them, drops anything at 0 or below and orders the rest highest first, then cheaper, then by name. `lib/autoBuild` starts the top-ranked item for a city on Auto that is building nothing. Rulesets act on the flag from their `BuildingComplete` / `BuildingCancelled` rules (civ-clone/web-renderer#194).
`localeCompare` follows the host's locale, so two clients could order equally scored, equally priced items differently. Compare by UTF-16 code unit instead, so the choice is the same on every client.

`buildItemInCity`'s random pick, weighed by the leader's `BuildWeight`, still decides between a unit and an improvement. When it lands on an improvement, or on nothing, the city builds the one `rankImprovements` puts first: core-city-build's `rankBuildItems` over the ruleset's `BuildPriority` rules, among the improvements it can finish within the policy's turns, weighed by `BuildWeight`. With nothing ranked, the pick stands. Barracks and City Walls go through the ranking, which only wants them with an enemy near. A city's yields are worked out once per choice and shared with `netShields`. Under a leader with no preference the ranking is the one a city on Auto uses; Ideology weighs improvements against Wonders.

Arena, 80 games of 150 turns against master: nothing at |t| >= 2 (score -0.36, t -1.1; advances -0.07, t -0.8). The choice is reached about 21 times a game (civ-clone/web-renderer#194). Needs core-city-build 0.1.13.

As civ-clone/web-renderer#194 specified: the top-ranked finishable improvement comes first, and the leader-weighted random pick only when nothing ranks. Before, a random pick that landed on a unit stood, so a starving city could keep building Warriors with a Granary ranked.

The random pick rarely runs now, so a Militaristic leader's lean towards units (#157) shows mostly in the quotas. Arena (80 games, against e972402): score +0.02 (t 0.0), units -0.57 (t -2.1), improvements +0.33 (t 3.8). Ranking units by need, so the lean returns through `BuildWeight` in the same ranking, is civ-clone/web-renderer#378. The #157 random-pick tests now set up a city that needs nothing.

localChanges: You can now put a city on Auto with the Auto button next to Change and Buy on the city screen, or next to View city in the production window, and press A on the city screen to turn it on or off. A city on Auto chooses its next improvement or Wonder by itself whenever a build finishes: a Granary when it's starving, an Aqueduct as it nears size 10, a Temple when its citizens are unhappy, a Marketplace or Library as its trade grows, and Barracks and City Walls first when an enemy is close. The city screen shows "Auto" under what it's building, and Stop Auto keeps the current build and hands the choice back to you (closes #194).
Computer players now choose their improvements the same way, by what each city needs, instead of picking one at random.

When one of your units attacks and loses, only that unit is destroyed now. The units it shared a tile with survive. A stack outside a city is still wiped out when its defender loses (closes #371).

log: `Attack` processes `Defeated` for a losing attacker as well as a defeated defender, passing itself as the third argument. `civ1-unit:unit/defeated/destroy-stack` now only applies when the defeated unit is not the action's unit, so a defeated attacker dies alone. Calls without an action keep the defender behaviour (civ-clone/web-renderer#371).

A ruleset declares its levels as `Difficulty` subclasses in `AvailableDifficultyRegistry`; a game holds its level as one `GameDifficulty` entity in `GameDifficultyRegistry`, so it is saved (civ-clone/web-renderer#173).

localChanges: A new game now asks for a difficulty level, Chieftain (easiest) to Emperor (toughest), after the size of the world and before the number of civilizations. It starts on the level you chose last time, or Prince (#173).

The level sets how many of your citizens are born content (six on Chieftain down to two on Emperor), and how soon a large empire makes them unhappy. It also sets what your research costs, and what the computer players pay for research, buildings and growth. On Chieftain you start with 50 gold.
Research costs twice as much from AD onwards, and more again when the leading civilization is ahead of schedule, as in Civilization.
The level is kept in your save and shown under the year. Loading a game saved before there were levels asks you to choose one.

The release notes, opened from the version number on the main menu, now show one entry per day instead of one per change, so a busy day no longer fills the list. Behind-the-scenes changes, such as tests and tidying up, are gathered under a heading you can expand (closes #355).

The options you change (auto end of turn, the unit edge margin, the map scale and stopping the map at the poles) are now remembered by your browser. They stay set when you reload the page or load a saved game (closes #343).

In Import Assets, "Replace existing" now does what its tick says. It starts ticked, so a re-import replaces the sprites you already have, and unticking it skips the ones that are complete (closes #341).

A city whose name isn't on its civilization's list, such as a Mongol Toronto, now shows as "Toronto" in messages and window titles like "What would you like to build in …?", instead of "Mongol.Toronto.name" (closes #337).
The welcome now reads "leader of England" rather than "leader of the England", and "leader of the Aztec Empire" for the Aztecs (closes #335).

The letters on busy units, such as F for fortified, are now drawn smoothly at the size the unit is shown at: on the map, in the city screen and on the action buttons. They're no longer enlarged into blocky pixels, and the units themselves keep their crisp look (closes #352).

Once you know Railroad, your automated Settlers build railroads on the roads around your cities wherever a railroad adds food, shields or trade, and so do the computer players' Settlers (closes #349).

log: lib/Unit/terrainWork and the TerrainWork strategy move here from simple-ai-client. terrainWork is split into a synchronous planTerrainJob, the walk, and a synchronous finishTerrainJob. TerrainWork takes the walk as its fourth constructor argument (simple-ai-client passes its move executor), so attempt() is the AI's path exactly as before: the settle check, plan, travel, finish.
order() is the standing order for automated Settlers (civ-clone/web-renderer#200): plan, followPath, finish, with no settle check, handing the unit back when there's no job or an enemy is near.
`TerrainImprovement` gains 'railroad', started with the unit's `buildRailroad` action, so a ruleset's `TerrainPolicy` can value railroads (civ-clone/web-renderer#349).

`civ1TerrainPolicy` offers a railroad on a tile with a road once the player has the Railroad advance. Its value is half of each of the tile's yields, rounded down, as `civ1-world`'s railroad `YieldModifier` (and v474.05's `GetCityResourceCount`) has it, weighed like the other jobs, so it's only offered where it adds something. Automated Settlers run the same policy (civ-clone/web-renderer#349).

The railroad tests cover a gain in each yield (Hills with a mine: +1 shield; Grassland with a road under the Republic: +1 food and +1 trade), and forget a tile's cached yields after building on it, as `civ1-world`'s `Built` rule does. The dependency floor is 0.1.1, the first release with the `railroad` job.

localChanges: Land military units, Diplomats, Caravans and ships can now be ordered to Explore (press E, or pick it from the unit's menu). They head into the unknown by themselves each turn and come back to you when there's nowhere left they can reach or another civilization's unit comes near (closes #198).

Settlers can now be set to Automate (press A). They build roads, irrigation and mines around your cities by themselves, one job after another, until there's nothing left worth doing or an enemy comes near. Selecting them stops it (closes #200).

log: `Automate` gives the worker the `Automated` busy rule, records the order in a `StrategyNote` (player, job, path as tiles) and runs the game's `TerrainWork` strategy (`base-strategy-terrain-work`, found in `game.strategies`) with the moves the worker has left. Once a job is under way the worker carries the job's own busy rule, and the note records its name and the job's `PendingEffect`, so the `TurnStart` rule (`Low` priority, each worker in its own try/catch) can tell a job still under way from one that finished (effect discharged) or one the player called off (busy cleared, or a different busy rule or newer effect: re-ordering a busy worker leaves the old effect owed). The worker is handed back when there is no job, another player's unit is near, or no strategy is registered. The busy factory is registered so saves load, and after a load the worker takes up the noted job and path. See civ-clone/web-renderer#200.

`Explore` gives the unit the `Exploring` busy rule, records the order in a `StrategyNote` (player and target tile, never a `Path`) and runs the game's `Explore` strategy (`base-strategy-explore`, found in `game.strategies`) with the moves the unit has left. A `TurnStart` rule at `Low` priority carries the order on each turn, each unit in its own try/catch. The unit is handed back (not busy, active, moves kept, note dropped) when the strategy's `order()` returns false, another player's unit is near, or no strategy is registered; giving it other orders ends the order. The busy factory is registered so saves load, and after a load the unit heads on for the noted target. See civ-clone/web-renderer#198.
