log: `getByPlayer` scanned every city on each call. A city's owner changes when it's captured, so `City#capture` calls core-registry's `keysChanged(this)` before processing `Captured` (whose rules may look the city up by its new owner), and `CityRegistry` keeps the index up to date. Lookups answer as the scan did, in registration order, however often a city has changed hands. Destroyed cities are still left out unless asked for. Needs core-registry ^0.1.6 (civ-clone/web-renderer#308).

From review: the other capture test only looked after `capture` returned, so it would still pass with `keysChanged` moved after the rules. This one records the lookups from inside a `Captured` rule, and fails if it is.

An entry filed by something that can change (a unit's tile, a city's owner) calls `keysChanged(this)` from `@civ-clone/core-registry/keysChanged`, and every registry holding it re-files it. `EntityRegistry` asks to be told for each entry while it holds it, once it has an index. Watchers are held weakly both ways: by entry in a `WeakMap`, and each registry through a `WeakRef` (reached via `globalThis`, so it compiles against an ES2019/ES2020 `lib`; strong where there's no `WeakRef`). A registry dropped without unregistering its entries is not kept alive by them.
`RegistryIndex` now:
remembers the key each entry was filed under, so it can take the entry out of that bucket after its key has changed (no more scanning every bucket);

keeps each bucket in registration order, the order of `entries()`, so a lookup answers in the same order as the scan it replaces however often an entry has moved. Previously a re-filed entry went to the end. For keys that never change, nothing is different;
finds an entry in its bucket by binary search on that order;
has `refile(entity)`, which touches only a bucket whose key changed.
`reindex(entity)` is `keysChanged(entity)`: the same re-file, now without a search. `includes` reads the order map rather than scanning.

From review. `refile` compared the filed and current keys with `===`, but `Map` matches keys with SameValueZero, under which `NaN` is the same key as `NaN`. An unchanged `NaN` key was taken out and put back, which moves the entry to the end of its bucket in a standalone `RegistryIndex` (one without a registration order). The keys are now compared as the `Map` does. The regression test fails with `===`.

From review. A registry collected without unregistering left its `WeakRef` in each entry's watcher set until that entry's keys changed or it was unwatched. So an entry that outlived many registries without ever changing key collected one dead reference per registry. The registries themselves were freed; only the small wrappers stayed. `watchKeys` already walks the set, so it now drops cleared references as it goes.
`getByTile`, `getByCity` and `getByPlayer` scanned every unit on each call. On a turn-247 save (huge map, ~1,000 units) they were ~17% of a turn between them.

A unit's tile, city and owner change, so `Unit`'s three setters (`setTile`, `setCity`, `transfer`) now call `keysChanged(this)`, and `UnitRegistry` asks to be told (`lib/keysChanged`, a `WeakMap` from unit to the registries holding it, so nothing outlives the unit) while a unit is registered with it. `transfer` says so before processing `Transferred`, whose rules may look the unit up.

Lookups give exactly what the scan gave, in the same order. Each bucket is kept in registration order, which is the order of `entries()`. Destroyed units are still left out at lookup. Keys are compared as they are, so `null` and `undefined` cities stay apart as they did under `===`. Units restored from a save are filed when `hydrate` registers them, after their fields are filled.
Tested by a seeded 2,000-step fuzz against the old scan, and in web-renderer: conformance is identical, all save/load/isolation suites pass, and turns are 15–22% shorter (civ-clone/web-renderer#308).

From review. A move re-filed the unit under its owner and home city too, which hadn't changed. Removal was a linear search and both steps shift the bucket, so a move cost work in proportion to everyone sharing those keys; the bucket of units with no home holds units from every player. Now only buckets whose key changed are touched, and a unit is found in its bucket by binary search on its registration order. 20,000 moves of one unit among 5,000 sharing an owner and no home: 275 ms to 10 ms.

Each unit's watchers were held strongly, so a registry dropped without unregistering its units stayed reachable through them. They're held by `WeakRef` now, reached through `globalThis` so it compiles against the renderer's ES2020 `lib`, with a strong reference as the fallback where there's no `WeakRef`. A test checks that a dropped registry is collected; it needs `--expose-gc` and skips without it. Run with it, it fails with strong references and passes with weak ones.

The mechanism moved to core-registry 0.1.6, where `CityRegistry` (a city's owner changes on capture) and others can share it. `UnitRegistry` is now three `this.index(...)` declarations, and `Unit`'s setters call core-registry's `keysChanged`. Home cities of `null` and `undefined` are keyed by stand-in symbols, since the index leaves those keys out but the scan compared them with `===`. `lib/keysChanged` is removed before it was ever published.

When the next step of a path can't be taken, `moveUnit` drops it and tries the one after, which is two tiles away, then three, and so on. `unit.actions()` on a tile that isn't a neighbour runs civ1-unit's `goto` criterion, a full path search, and can never offer a `Move` (every kind of move needs `isNeighbouringTile`). log: A computer player's Settlers with no city site it can reach, no terrain job and no step worth taking now joins one of its player's cities, as v474.05's computer players have a spare Settlers do (OpenCivOne `AIEngine.cs`, L1468-1483), instead of stepping back and forth at random: at once in the city it stands in, or else it heads for the nearest of the player's cities it could join and joins on arriving (civ-clone/web-renderer#243, #230).

Which cities it could join comes from the ruleset (`joinableCity` and the `CanJoinCity` rules, Civ1's size-10 limit) and whether the unit may join from the rule that offers `JoinCity`, so the generic code holds neither. With no city it could join, it waits in the city it's in or the nearest one.

Settlers with nothing to do now join a city, so cities that kept building Settlers up to the cap with no city site and no terrain job for them spent the shields only to have the citizen given back. Civ1's production now builds Settlers only when there's a city site on the board they could walk to from the city, or a terrain job there that no unit of the player's has claimed (`hasOpenTerrainJob`).
docs: say plainly what v474.05's computer players do with spare Settlers

`hasOpenTerrainJob` counted a job on the terrain policy's score alone, but the policy scores jobs no worker has an action for, such as irrigation with no water beside the tile (civ-clone/simple-ai-client#28 review). A player whose only open jobs were like that kept passing the production gate, built Settlers that found no job and no site, and joined them to a city again.

`chooseTerrainJob` now remembers each job it passes over because the worker has no action for it, per player, when the worker had moves left: with none, a unit is offered no actions at all. `hasOpenTerrainJob` leaves those out. A job is forgotten after `UNDOABLE_TURNS` (20) turns, or as soon as the improvements on or around its tile, or the player's advances, change.

Loading into any other `Game`, `gameForLoad`'s included, it is not: the effect was in the loading game's registry, and a unit saved part-way through fortifying refused to load with `MissingPendingEffectError` (civ-clone/web-renderer#245).

localChanges: A Settlers unit standing in one of your cities can now join it, as in Civ1: press B, or pick Join city from the unit's menu, and the city grows by one while the Settlers are used up. Only cities smaller than size 10 can be joined (#243).
Computer players no longer flood the map with Warriors: they build explorers only while there is land a unit could reach, and only units their cities can support (closes #229).
Computer players now spend the gold they hold above a reserve on finishing their cities' improvements, and on a defender for a city that has none (closes #233).

Computer players now choose their government the way Civ1's do, by their leader's personality and their situation, rather than always taking Monarchy (closes #231). Those that take The Republic can see more unrest in their cities from units away from home (#242).

Computer players' fighting units and ships with nothing left to do now wait in one of their cities, or are disbanded, instead of walking back and forth between the same tiles. Settlers with nothing to do can still wander (#230).

Computer players' Settlers with no city site left to settle now irrigate, mine and build roads on the land their cities work, and Settlers busy with that work no longer hold their player back from building more to found new cities (#234).
A computer player's unit that garrisons one of its cities now becomes that city's unit, so the city it defends is the one that supports it.
Computer players' explorers no longer stop for the rest of the turn when they reach the edge of the known map, and go straight on to their next destination.

log: The repository files, MIT licence, TypeScript and Prettier settings, the test tooling the newer engine packages use, and the standard build workflow (pnpm install, prettier --check, compile with --force, fail on stale or uncommitted output, ts-mocha). The JoinCity action follows on a branch, for civ-clone/web-renderer#243.

`JoinCity` grows the city by one through `CityGrowth.grow()`, so the ruleset's `Grow` rules assign the new citizen a worked tile (or make a specialist) and set the next growth cost, then destroys the unit and processes `Moved`, as `FoundCity` does. The food box is restored to what it held before the grow: `Grow` rules empty it (civ1-city) or half-fill it (a Granary), which is the cost of growing from food. In v474.05 the join (PlayerTurn.cs L701-730) only does `ActualSize++` and deletes the unit; the food count, shields and worked tiles are left as they were.

`joinableCity(unit, tile)` is the availability check: the unit's player's city on the tile, provided every applicable `CanJoinCity` rule returns true. The size limit (Civ1: under 10) is a `CanJoinCity` rule in the ruleset, and which units may join is decided by the rule that offers the action, so neither is fixed here.
The action holds no state after `perform`, and nothing keeps a reference to it, so a save needs no new class registration.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#243.

`Action.forUnit` rebuilds an action as `(from, to, unit, ruleRegistry)`, which put the `RuleRegistry` in `JoinCity`'s `city` slot (Copilot, on #1). `forUnit` is overridden to pass the city and both registries on.

A test now saves a game after a join and loads it with core-save-game: the city's size and food box, its worked tiles and the destroyed unit come back, and saving the loaded game writes the same entities. The action itself holds no state and is never saved.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#243.
A new scoped package is restricted unless it says otherwise, and `civ publish` takes `publishConfig.access` as the sign that a package belongs on npm rather than being consumed from GitHub.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#243.

`civ1-unit:unit/action/join-city` offers `JoinCity` (from base-unit-action-join-city, through library-unit) to a Settlers with moves left on the tile of one of its player's cities, as `joinableCity` decides. `found-city` is never offered on a city tile, so the two can share the `b` key.

`civ1-unit:unit/can-join-city/size-limit` is the Civ1 limit, a `CanJoinCity` rule with `joinCitySizeLimit = 10`: a city under size 10 can be joined; v474.05 shows the `*ADDCITY` warning otherwise (OpenCivOne PlayerTurn.cs L701-730).

`action` takes the `CityGrowthRegistry` as a new last parameter, and `registerRules` passes `game.cityGrowth` to it and to `canJoinCity`. Nothing new needs registering for saves: the action holds no state.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#243.

56 `base-unit-*` and `base-player-action-*` packages were declared but never imported here: every one is imported through `@civ-clone/library-unit` (`Actions`, `PlayerActions`, `Types`, `Units`, `UnitImprovements`), which declares them itself. The ones imported directly (embark, join-city, land-aircraft, sleep) stay.

The workflow ran `npm install` on Node 18 and stopped at install whenever a dependency had only just been published. It is now the standard one from core-city: pnpm without a lock file on Node 22, `prettier:check` with `--check` (it listed files rather than failing on them), and a compile that fails if the committed `.js` / `.d.ts` / `.js.map` are stale. The unused `package-lock.json` goes too (civ-clone/web-renderer#66).

`registerDelayedAction` registers its `Busy` factory at import, closing over the singleton `PendingEffectRegistry`, `RuleRegistry` and `Turn`. Loading into `defaultGame` that is the right game. Loading into any other `Game`, such as `core-save-game`'s `gameForLoad`, `hydrate` registers the restored effects in that game's registry, and the factory still searched the singleton. The only match there was the saved game's effect, owed to the saved unit rather than the restored one, so a unit part-way through fortifying refused to load with `MissingPendingEffectError`, naming an effect the file contained (civ-clone/web-renderer#245).

`BusyRegistry.rebuild(identity, unit, context)` now hands the factory a `BusyContext` (`pendingEffects`, `rules`, `turn`, named after `Game`'s slots so a loader can pass the `Game`). The delayed-action factory reads the effect from it, builds the rule against those registries, and registers its handler on the loading registry if that registry does not know it, so the restored unit can still finish. The context is optional, in the `BusyFactory` type too, so a factory can still be called as `factory(unit)`; without one it behaves as before.

The rebuilt rule also builds its action only when the work finishes. `delayedBusy` accepts a function for the action. Building the action during the load took the next `Fortify` id from a counter `hydrate` had just restored, so saving a loaded game again wrote a different file.
CI installs with pnpm and no lock file (civ-clone/web-renderer#66), so the npm lock file only went stale.

The Node 18 / `npm i` workflow is replaced by the standard one (civ-clone/web-renderer#66): pnpm install with web-renderer's settings, `prettier --check`, `ts:compile -- --force`, fail on stale or uncommitted compiled output, then the tests. `prettier:check` gets `--check`, so it fails on unformatted files instead of printing them.
`core-player` and `core-rule` were imported (SetHomeCity, SneakAttack, SneakCaptureCity) but undeclared, so they're dependencies now.
The package had no tests, so it gets one: each of its modules exports only classes, each under its own name.

`JoinCity`, from the new base-unit-action-join-city package, is re-exported from `Actions` like the other unit actions, so civ1-unit can offer it to Settlers in their own city (civ-clone/web-renderer#243).
civ-clone/web-renderer#229. In the explorer branch of `buildItemInCity`:
only frontier tiles a land unit could walk to from the city count (`lib/City/explorers`), so the coast of another continent no longer keeps cities building explorers for ever;
the quota is capped by the policy's new `maxExplorers` as well as per city;
explorers are land units that can fight outside the player's cities, on an explore mission or not, plus those on order.

No unit but a missing defender (or martial-law unit) and Settlers is started when supporting it would leave the city no shields to spare (`lib/Civ1/unitSupport`, Civ1's support rules: free up to the city's size under Anarchy and Despotism, a shield each otherwise).
Settlers on order count against the Settlers cap, now the policy's `settlers`.

civ-clone/web-renderer#229. With Settlers on order counted against a cap of 3 for any number of cities, players had 2.3 fewer cities than the baseline at turn 300 in the arena (40 games, t = -2.3). The cap is now the policy's `settlers` (3) plus `settlersPerCity` (0.5) per city, rounded down, still counting those on order.
test: show Settlers on order counting towards the cap with three cities

The comment said Diplomats and Caravans need no support, as in v474.05, but `civ1-city`'s cost rules charge for them (both are `Fortifiable`), and `unitSupport` follows those rules. A test now checks it against the rules' own yields.

`isFoundingSettlers` says which of a player's units are Settlers for founding cities, and so count towards the policy's `settlers` and keep their home city from building more: all Settlers, as before. Settlers kept for terrain work (civ-clone/web-renderer#234) can be left out there in one line.

civ-clone/web-renderer#229. `BuildExplorerShip` runs ahead of `ChooseProduction`, so `explorerShipFor` now applies the same check: no ship that would leave the city no shields to spare once it supported it. The support cost comes from a new `Knowledge#unitSupport`, Civ1's being `lib/Civ1/unitSupport`, which `buildItemInCity` now reads there too.
In the arena the check never fired: 80 games of 150 turns and 40 of 300 against the commit before play identically.

civ-clone/web-renderer#233. A new `AfterTurn` strategy, `Strategies/City/SpendTreasury`, registered after `PreventDisorder` and `TradeRates`, buys whole builds at the ruleset's price (`PlayerTreasury#cost`/`#buy`) while the treasury stays at or over the policy's reserve (`lib/City/spendTreasury`): a defender or martial-law unit a city wants first, then an improvement or Settlers (in a city over size 1) the city would still take `minTurns` or more to finish, most turns saved per gold first, then a Wonder with no more than `wonderRemaining` of it left. Nothing is bought before the city has put a shield into it, as in v474.05.

Civ1's policy (`lib/Civ1/spending`) keeps 30 gold plus 10 per city, and buys builds of 5 turns or more and Wonders a quarter from done. A reserve of the turn + 100 (where v474.05's rates routine adds a step of science) was tried first: most players then never spent by turn 150, and it built fewer improvements and grew less, for no more advances by turn 300.

Anything that was neither a unit nor a Wonder was bought as an improvement, so Civ1's spaceship parts (`civ1-spaceship` prices them) would have been too. Improvements are now recognised as `CityImprovement`s, for which `@civ-clone/core-city-improvement` moves from devDependencies to dependencies.
test: buy an improvement before a Wonder that is nearly done

civ-clone/web-renderer#231. `lib/Civ1/government` follows OpenCivOne's `AIEngine.cs` `F0_25fb_0004_RecalculateStatsAndPolicies` (L340-366): The Republic, if known, while `republicScore` is 0 or more (a point per worked tile giving trade, less 7 - Ideology, or 5 - Ideology with a Marketplace, for each unit that can attack away from its city: `CityWorker.cs` L1918-1925 and L3757-3760); otherwise Communism with more than 10 cities; otherwise Monarchy. Democracy is never chosen, as in the original.

Where the original changes government on the spot, here each change is a revolution with Anarchy: a player leaves Despotism as soon as it knows any other government and never returns to it by choice (the original's units-upkeep rule for Despotism is left out), and otherwise waits `revolutionTurns` (40) after its last revolution before another. With none of the original's choices available, the first known of Monarchy, Communism and The Republic.
`Dependencies` gains `cityImprovementRegistry`, for the Marketplace.

Civ1's Democracy needs Philosophy and Literacy, not The Republic, so it can be the first government a player learns. The fallback already took it then (rather than stay in Despotism, as v474.05 would); the comments and README said it never does. A test now covers it.
test: pin the wait between revolutions to exactly 40 turns
docs: say plainly where the government choice departs from v474.05

A unit with no mission, no path and no neighbouring step scoring above zero used to take the greedy step anyway, picked at random among equal zero scores, so it paced between tiles for ever (civ-clone/web-renderer#230).

`MissionAndMove` now returns `false` for such a unit (aircraft excepted, unchanged), and `moveUnit` takes `{ wander }`: without it, the greedy step only takes steps scoring above zero, and stops otherwise.

New last unit strategy `StandDown` (`lib/Unit/standDown.ts`), after `MissionAndMove`: a land defender goes to the nearest reachable own city that still wants a defender or a martial-law unit (`City/defence`), counting units already heading there; otherwise the unit is disbanded if the ruleset's `StandDownPolicy` says so; otherwise it waits (`NoOrders`, not fortified, so it takes the next mission that comes up) in its city, or heads for the nearest reachable own city (a ship to the sea beside it and then into port), or fortifies where it stands.
Civ1's policy (`lib/Civ1/standDown.ts`): disband when the home city pays `UnitSupportProduction` for the unit and its net shields are at most 0.
`scoreUnitMove`'s discovery term counts only unknown tiles of terrain the unit can enter (`terrainFor` in `lib/Unit/reachable.ts`).
Tests in `tests/StandDown.test.ts` over a small Civ1 game (`tests/lib/unitGame.ts`); `tsconfig.json` now excludes all of `tests`.
From Copilot's review of #21:

`StandDown` follows its path with `moveUnit`'s new `stopAtPathEnd`, then gives `NoOrders`: a unit that reached its city with moves to spare took the greedy step after the path ended, so a goody hut or other positive step beside the city pulled it straight out again.
A city's defender shortfall is set against the defenders on their way there (`isDefender`), not every unit whose path ends there, so a ship going into port no longer cancels it.
Test: a Horseman sent to a city wanting a defender, arriving with a move to spare beside a hut, stays (fails before: it took the hut).
Settlers only improved a tile they happened to stand on; once city sites ran out they wandered (civ-clone/web-renderer#234).

`lib/Unit/terrainWork.ts` (generic): a worker's terrain job is the tile, on the player's cities' tiles, reachable and unclaimed (no other unit's job, target or path end), whose improvement the ruleset's `TerrainPolicy` values most per turn of walking plus work; the top few are checked with `unit.actions(tile, tile)` against what the worker could do there. The worker walks there (`moveUnit` with `stopAtPathEnd`), starts work on arrival if it has moves left, and picks the next job once the policy no longer values the old one. Jobs are kept per player beside its `Memory`.

`Strategies/Unit/TerrainWork.ts`, registered after `FoundCapital` and before `WorkerTurn`: takes or continues a job for a worker with no site target, not standing on a site, and with no site it can reach, or while the player has fewer workers on jobs than `workersWanted`; until work starts, a worker goes back to settling (job dropped) once that changes. Handles the action only when the worker has a job to get on with.

`civ1TerrainPolicy` (`lib/Civ1/terrain.ts`): irrigation, mines and roads valued by what `civ1-world`'s `Yield` rules add per government (Grassland and River irrigation add nothing under Despotism; mines replace irrigation and the reverse), weighted food 2, shields 1.5, trade 1, x1.5 for what the city has at most 1 of to spare, x0.5 for a tile the city doesn't work; work turns from `civ1-unit`'s movement costs. One terrain worker per eight cities: each counts towards the three Settlers `buildItemInCity` builds at most, so is one fewer settling.
Tests in `tests/TerrainWork.test.ts`.
From Copilot's review of #25:

`TerrainWork` asks every worker it's offered whether it should settle instead, not only one away from its job's tile: a worker is offered only while it isn't at work, so standing on the job tile (arrived with no moves left) didn't mean work had started.

`chooseTerrainJob` checks the ranked jobs until one the worker could do, not only the best 5 (each tile is still asked about once), so a list topped by irrigation with no water beside it no longer leaves the worker with nothing.
`dropTerrainJob` forgets the path to a dropped job, so `WorkerTurn` doesn't follow it to a job the worker no longer has.
Civ1's policy comment and the README say the `SHORT` weight applies to food and shields, as the code does.
Tests for each of the three, each failing before.

With units no longer wandering (civ-clone/web-renderer#230), a unit whose path ended with moves left and no step worth taking stood still for the rest of the turn: an explorer that reached the edge of the known map waited there a turn before its next mission. `moveUnit` takes an `onIdle` callback, asked at most three times a turn, and `MissionAndMove` uses it to assign the unit's next mission straight away.

Explorers are now exempt from the rule that no unit is started which would leave its city no shields to spare (civ-clone/web-renderer#229), as missing defenders and Settlers are. With units that have nothing left to do standing down rather than wandering (civ-clone/web-renderer#230), explorers are all that explores, and keeping them to cities with shields to spare left players with less explored by turn 300 (t -2.8 against 2a2fb02 in the arena). The explorer quota itself (reachable land, at most 6) is unchanged. The Despotism upkeep tests now use the random pick, which the rule still governs.

A computer player's unit that takes up station in one of its cities other than its home, fortified there by `Garrison` or left waiting there by `StandDown`, now makes that city its home (the engine's `SetHomeCity`), under any government, so a city's defenders are its own units. Units passing through or on their way somewhere keep their home. `lib/Unit/homeCity` decides it; a unit stays homed where it is when the city couldn't support another unit without going to zero net shields (`Knowledge#unitSupport`). Martial law counts the units in a city whatever their home, so it is unaffected.
docs: describe re-homing garrisons and the next mission after a path ends

`StandDown` disbanded a unit whose home city paid for it with no shields to spare before it could make the city it was waiting in its home, so a unit the receiving city could have supported was disbanded instead. It now re-homes first, and the disband policy weighs the new home.

`chooseTerrainJob` judges reachability by terrain alone, so the best job can have no path; `terrainWork` then dropped it and gave up, and chose the same job again the next turn, for ever. It now tries the next best jobs, up to `PATH_TRIES` (3) path searches a turn, and remembers the tiles it found no path to for `UNPATHABLE_TURNS` (10) turns, so it doesn't search for them again.

`spendTreasury` bought any `Fortifiable` unit at the top priority while its city wanted a defender or a martial-law unit, so a Diplomat or Caravan (no defence, and no attack for martial law) was bought and the city stayed short. A purchase is now a `'defender'` only for a unit type that can defend (`isDefenderType`, by the ruleset's base yields) when the city is short of defenders, or one martial law would use (`MartialLawPolicy#wouldUse`; Civ1's: any attack, as `civ1-city-happiness`'s `keepsMartialLaw`) when it is short of those. `wantsUnit` is split into `wantsDefender` and `wantsMartialLawUnit`.

A terrain worker's cache of tiles it found no path to expired all at once, UNPATHABLE_TURNS after the first was added, so a tile that failed late in that window was searched for again almost immediately. Each tile now keeps the turn it failed and is forgotten UNPATHABLE_TURNS after that turn (civ-clone/web-renderer#234).

A game saved part way through a computer player's turn starts that turn over when it is loaded, and `SurveyTargets` surveyed again, of the world as it stood at the save rather than as the turn began. web-renderer's load check saves at `turn:start`, after player 1's `BeforeTurn` survey has already run, and its harness puts a Trireme with a Warrior aboard on the map in between, revealing five tiles. The loaded game's board therefore offered different targets. Until b7cd557 nothing asked for a second mission in that turn, so it went unnoticed; the `onIdle` re-mission gave the Trireme a different tile (13,11 instead of 14,12 for seed 1) and the replay diverged. Seed 5's long-standing replay failure is the same thing.

`surveyTargets` now keeps the board in a `StrategyNote` (saved with the game), holding `Memory#targets` itself, so a save takes the board as the turn has left it. A memory that has never surveyed (`surveyedTurn` null), for a player whose note says the board was already surveyed this turn, takes that board up instead of surveying. Uninterrupted play is unchanged: the first survey of a game finds no note, and every later one finds a memory that has surveyed before.

isFoundingSettlers (lib/Civ1/buildItemInCity.ts) now leaves out Settlers holding a terrain job (terrainJobs(memory), lib/Unit/terrainWork.ts), so terrain workers neither count towards the policy's 3 + cities / 2 founding Settlers nor keep their home city from building another (civ-clone/web-renderer#234).
Test (tests/production.test.ts), failing before: a city whose own Settlers is on a terrain job, with the cap otherwise full, builds Settlers, and doesn't once the job is dropped.

isFoundingSettlers (lib/Civ1/buildItemInCity.ts) leaves out Settlers on terrain jobs only up to civ1TerrainPolicy.workersWanted, the first to take their jobs; any more count as founding Settlers again. With all of them left out ("fix: Settlers on terrain jobs don't count against the Settlers cap"), every Settlers with no reachable site took a job and freed its city to build another: over 40 games of 300 turns against fix/lanes-compose, players built 28 Settlers rather than 21, net shields fell 6.7 (t -3.7) and score 11 (t -2.9). Limited to the quota, power +36 (t 1.8), cities +0.6 (t 2.1), advances +1.3 (t 2.2), irrigated tiles +4.9 (t 2.2) (civ-clone/web-renderer#234).

Test (tests/production.test.ts), failing before: with eight cities (one terrain worker wanted) the first Settlers on a job is left out and a second counts; once the first drops its job, the second is left out.
Keeps civ1TerrainPolicy at one terrain worker per eight cities, and records what the arena found for one per four and per six with terrain workers left out of the cap (civ-clone/web-renderer#234).
From Copilot's review of #27.

localChanges: test: the arena counts the shields cities make, what their units cost, and what's left
test: the arena counts trade, improved tiles, where units end up and units pacing back and forth

Computer players now choose what to build by how long it will take: a city only starts a unit, an improvement, a ship or a Wonder it can finish in reasonable time at the shields it has left after supporting its units, and picks units for their strength per shield rather than the strongest it knows. They finish many more improvements as a result, and start fewer Wonders (#212).

Martial law now works as it does in Civ1: up to three units in a city each keep one unhappy citizen content, only units that can attack count, and it applies after Temples, Colosseums and Cathedrals have done their part (#224).
Entertainers now come out of a city's content citizens before its unhappy ones, as in Civ1, so a large city's unrest can always be calmed by taking enough citizens off the land (#224).

log: Checked against OpenCivOne's decompile of the city happiness routine (`src/Game/CodeObjects/CityWorker.cs`, L1444-1575), martial law differed in three ways (civ-clone/web-renderer#224):
The cap is 3 units (`if (attackUnitCount > 3) attackUnitCount = 3`), not 4.

A unit counts if its type's attack strength isn't 0, not if it's `Fortifiable`: Diplomats no longer count, ships and aircraft do. Only the city owner's units count, as the original walks that player's units on the city's square.

It applies after the Colosseum, Cathedral and Temple (and the Oracle and Michelangelo's), so it calms what they leave. The rule now has `Priority(3500)`, after every `Low` improvement and Wonder rule here and in civ1-wonder, and before Shakespeare's Theatre (4000). The net unhappiness is the same either way; what changes is how many units the `MartialLaw` yields say are in use, which the city screen and the computer players read.

The governments are unchanged. `martialLaw.ts` exports them (`martialLawGovernments`), the cap (`martialLawUnitLimit`) and the unit test (`keepsMartialLaw`) so consumers don't repeat them. The rule has an id, `civ1-city-happiness:city/cost/martial-law`.
Not modelled: the original also counts the two `FirstFortifiedCityUnits` slots in the city record, which the engine has no equivalent of.

Tests: the governments and cap; 3 of 4 Warriors used; no more units than unhappy citizens; a Trireme counts, Settlers and a Diplomat don't; none under a Republic; with a Temple (2 with Mysticism) and 3 Warriors against 4 unhappy, the Temple calms 2 and martial law the other 2. The existing martial-law tests in `yield.test.ts` use Warriors with civ1-unit's yields, and the cap is now 3.
civ-clone/web-renderer#224 asked whether Entertainers can calm a size-8 city with 3 unhappy citizens. In v474.05 they can (3 of them), and here they couldn't with any number.

v474.05 (OpenCivOne's decompile, `CityWorker.cs`: the happiness routine and `F0_1d12_6dfe_AdjustHappyUnhappyCitizens`, whose `size` argument is the specialist count) clamps happy + unhappy to the working citizens right after setting the base unhappiness, while nobody is happy yet: so specialists come out of the content citizens, then the unhappy ones. Luxuries come after, and each excess happy face cancels an unhappy one (`H--, U--`), so a point of luxury makes a content citizen happy or, with none left, an unhappy one content.

`calculateCitizenState` followed Rome on 640K a Day (p249): it applied Happiness first and then took specialists from the content citizens, then the happy ones, then the unhappy. Once the content citizens ran out each Entertainer's own luxury made a happy citizen that the next specialist removed, so they never calmed a city.

It now takes specialists out first (content, then unhappy), then applies Happiness. Its loop also no longer spends a point it doesn't have: with one point left at an unhappy citizen it made them content and then happy as well.
Size 8, 3 unhappy, k Entertainers (k Happiness): k = 3 gives 2 happy and 2 unhappy, calm, as in v474.05 (H 3 + U 3 > 5 working: H 2, U 2); k = 2 stays in disorder in both.

Not changed, and still different from v474.05: the engine nets every Unhappiness yield before assigning moods, where the original applies luxuries, then improvements, then martial law, then Wonders, clamping in between. Totals of happy minus unhappy mostly agree; the split between them can differ.

Tests: the specialist order and the single spend in `calculateCitizenState`; disorder with 2 and 3 Entertainers in a size-8 city with 3 unhappy; the old "specialists take the happy citizens" disorder case is now calm.
chore: CI compiles and fails on stale compiled output, as core-strategy's does (civ-clone/web-renderer#66)
core-terrain-feature and simple-world-generator are imported by nothing here; civ1-city and core-science were listed in both dependencies and dev dependencies (civ-clone/web-renderer#66).

`lib/Civ1/martialLaw.ts` repeated civ1-city-happiness's martial law, 4 units under Anarchy, Communism, Despotism or Monarchy, because the rule kept them in its own closure. civ1-city-happiness now applies v474.05's (civ-clone/web-renderer#224: 3 units that can attack, after the city's improvements and Wonders) and exports `martialLawGovernments` and `martialLawUnitLimit`; the policy imports them.

Which units martial law uses is still read from the engine's `MartialLaw` yields (`martialLawUnitsIn`), so the AI counts the units the engine counts: no Diplomats, but a ship in the city. A comment in `City/defence` no longer says martial law comes first.

Tests (over the new civ1-city-happiness): a size-10 city wants 3 units, not 4; with a Temple martial law only uses two of three Warriors; a Diplomat doesn't count, so a city with two Warriors and a Diplomat builds a third unit.
Needs civ1-city-happiness's fix/martial-law-fidelity merged (the import doesn't exist before it) before CI can pass.
`getOffensiveUnit`/`getDefensiveUnit` took the unit with the most Attack/Defence whatever it cost, so a size-1 city making 1 shield could start a 40-shield Catapult (civ-clone/web-renderer#212).

`lib/City/buildTime` (generic) works out turns to finish a build item at the city's net shields (Production yields after unit support), counting the shields stored: 0 if already paid for, Infinity at 0 net shields.

`chooseUnit` replaces `getUnitByYield`: of the units the city can finish within `ProductionPolicy.buildTurns.unit` (10), the most strength per shield, then the most strength, then the cheapest. Units with no strength are ignored; obsolete units are never offered by the ruleset. Only a defender for the city itself falls back, when nothing is that soon, to the soonest (then cheapest); an attacker, or a defender for another undefended city, isn't started at all.

Tests: an attacker it can finish over a stronger one it can't; the stronger one once stored shields bring it within reach; a defender it can finish over a stronger one; the cheapest defender at 0 net shields. The existing attacker test gets 2 shields so it can finish Horsemen.

`SimpleAIClient#unitDestroyed` chose the emergency rebuild with `defaultProductionPolicy`, not the policy the player's `ChooseProduction` strategy uses (civ-clone/web-renderer#212). Harmless while every player has the default, wrong once #157 gives them their own.

`ChooseProduction#choose(player, city)` now does what `attempt` did, and the client asks the first `ChooseProduction` in its own strategy registry (kept as `_strategies`, as `StrategyAIClient`'s is private), so the rebuild uses the strategy's policy, knowledge and registries. With no `ChooseProduction` registered it falls back to the default policy as before.
Tests: a policy willing to wait 20 turns rebuilds a Phalanx and is asked for the player once; with no `ChooseProduction` the default policy rebuilds Warriors.

The explorer branch built the cheapest land unit that can fight whatever the city made, so a city on 0 net shields started Warriors it would never finish (civ-clone/web-renderer#212). It now only takes an explorer the city can finish within `buildTurns.unit`, and otherwise moves on to its other choices. The quota itself is unchanged (#229).
Test: a city on 0 net shields with land to explore doesn't start Warriors. The existing explorer test gets the 1 shield Warriors need.

Cities on 0 net shields started Settlers they would never finish (civ-clone/web-renderer#212). Settlers are now only chosen when the city can finish them within `ProductionPolicy.buildTurns.settlers` (20).
Tests: a size-2 city making 1 net shield (40 turns) doesn't start Settlers; one making 2 (20 turns) does.

`shouldBuildWonder` had no minimum: a city on 1 net shield started the Oracle at 4/300 (civ-clone/web-renderer#212). A Wonder is now only chosen when the city can finish it within `ProductionPolicy.buildTurns.wonder` (40) and makes at least `wonderShields` (5) net shields, however many it has stored. `shouldBuildWonder` compares net shields through `lib/City/buildTime`, which now takes the net shields when the caller has them.
Tests: no Colossus (200) at 4 net shields; none at 4 net shields with 190 stored. The existing Wonder tests get the 5 shields they now need.

The Wonder was picked at random from everything available, so a player with no ships could start the Lighthouse (civ-clone/web-renderer#212). `lib/Civ1/wonders` judges whether a Wonder does anything for the player: not if it's obsolete (civ1-wonder's `isObsolete`, which Civ1 applies as soon as anyone has the obsoleting advance), and the Lighthouse and Magellan's Expedition only for a player with a ship. Only useful Wonders are drawn from. civ1-wonder moves from dev dependencies to dependencies.
Tests: no obsolete Colossus; no Lighthouse without ships; the Lighthouse with a Trireme.

`BuildExplorerShip` took the cheapest ship whatever the city made, so a city on 0 net shields started a Frigate it would never finish (civ-clone/web-renderer#212). `explorerShipFor` now also requires the city to finish the ship within `explorerShipTurns` (20) at its net shields; its last argument overrides that.
Test: no Trireme (40 shields) at 1 net shield. The other ship tests give the coastal city 2 net shields, enough for a Trireme in 20 turns.

The last choice, a random pick of the remaining units and improvements, ignored cost, so a city could spend 80 turns on City Walls (civ-clone/web-renderer#212). It now draws only from what the city can finish within `buildTurns.unit` (10) for a unit or `buildTurns.improvement` (40) for an improvement, still with one draw per call.

When the city can finish none of them it builds the cheapest improvement worth having, rather than drawing from everything: units come last, as they'd cost support the city doesn't have, and Barracks and City Walls just before them, as they're only worth building on purpose.
Tests: at 1 net shield no draw picks City Walls (120 shields); at 0 net shields the first and last draws both build a Temple, not Warriors or Barracks.
At 150 turns over 40 games against 7d643a2, the first limits cost more than they saved (civ-clone/web-renderer#212):

Settlers within 20 turns cost cities (-0.80, t -2.9) and power (-29, t -2.4); 40 turns was still worse than no limit. Settlers are now built by any city that makes net shields, however long they take (`buildTurns.settlers` Infinity), so only a city that would never finish them is stopped.

A Wonder within 40 turns at 5 net shields stopped almost every Wonder: Wonders built -0.17 to -0.20 (t -3.5 to -4.1), score -3 to -6. Now 100 turns at 2 net shields, which still keeps a 1-shield city off a 300-shield Wonder.
`finishesWithin(turns, limit)` in `lib/City/buildTime` makes every limit check say no for a city making no net shields, even with no limit.
Tests: Settlers at 1 net shield, not at 0; no Pyramids (300) at 2 net shields, the Colossus (200) at 2; no Wonder at 1 net shield even with 190 stored.

Two earlier commits on this branch kept a city off Settlers it couldn't finish soon: first within 20 turns, then only at 0 net shields. Both cost the player in the arena (civ-clone/web-renderer#212), against 7d643a2:
20 turns, 40 games x 150 turns: cities -0.80 (t -2.9), power -29 (t -2.4).
0 net shields only, 80 x 150: score -3.1 (t -2.7), gold -56 (t -5.6); the same with no Wonder limit: score -2.7 (t -2.4).
No Settlers limit at all, otherwise the same: score -0.4, gold -17, both n.s.; advances and explored better.

A city's net shields when it chooses aren't what it makes over the next turns (it reassigns workers, and grows), and expansion is worth the wait. So Settlers are chosen as before this branch, and `buildTurns.settlers` is gone.

Once the random pick only drew what a city can finish, cities finished far more improvements (civ-clone/web-renderer#212), and Barracks and City Walls are only worth building on purpose: the fallback already put them after every other improvement. They're now left out of the random pick too (`onPurposeOnly`).
Test: at 3 net shields with Masonry, where both are within the improvement limit, no draw picks either.
test: say the Wonder test's city is within the 100-turn limit, not 40

localChanges: After loading a saved game, ships could no longer take units aboard or put them ashore, and a computer player that owned a ship stopped taking its turns. Ships, and the computer players who own them, now work after a load, including in games saved before this fix (closes #228).
A computer player's ship carrying a unit onto a tile that an enemy city was working no longer makes that ship lose its turn (#225).

log: `civ1-city:unit/moved/release-occupied-worked-tile` read the tile's `WorkedTile` in its criteria and again in its effect, assuming nothing changed in between. `RuleRegistry#process` checks every rule's criteria before running any effect, and `civ1-unit:unit/moved/move-cargo` (an earlier effect) moves the transport's cargo onto the same tile. Each cargo unit's own `Moved` rules release the tile, so by the time this rule's effect ran for the transport, `getByTile` returned null and `workedTile.city()` threw a TypeError (civ-clone/web-renderer#225: a Trireme carrying a Catapult, seed 15 at 300 turns).

The two views of "worked" never disagreed: the effect acted on a stale answer. The rule now looks the tile up once more in its effect, with the same test as the criterion (another player's city works it, not as its centre), and does nothing when an earlier effect has released it.
The test moves a real Trireme with a Warrior aboard through civ1-unit's `Moved` rules, registered ahead of this package's as in a game.
chore: CI compiles and fails on stale compiled output, as core-strategy's does (civ-clone/web-renderer#66)

`Rules/City/{captured,created,grow,shrink,tile-reassigned}.ts` import core-player-world, and `Rules/City/cost.ts` the three base-city-yield-*-support packages, but those were dev dependencies, so a consumer only had them through other packages. They're dependencies now. civ1-unit and civ1-world were listed in both; simple-world-generator was used by nothing (civ-clone/web-renderer#66).

`Game.inject` gives `_transportRegistry` the game's `transports` and `_transportRuleRegistry` its `rules`, now that core-unit-transport declares both transient. Without them a ship came back from a load holding plain arrays, and `cargo()` threw (civ-clone/web-renderer#228).
core-strategy's compile step: `ts:compile -- --force`, so a fresh checkout's timestamps can't skip the compile, then fail on stale or uncommitted output.

It recorded core-city ^0.1.0 at 0.1.12 against package.json's ^0.1.16, and CI installs with --no-frozen-lockfile and rewrites it anyway, so it locked nothing. Like the other engine repos, CI now tests what a consumer resolves.

core-strategy 0.1.6 accepts the generator but stores nothing, because ties are ordered by registration rather than by a draw. The stale pnpm-lock.yaml held core-strategy at an older version, which hid this; without the lock file, CI resolves what a consumer gets.

`_transportRegistry` and `_transportRuleRegistry` were saved as state: each ship carried a dump of every rule, and came back from a load holding plain arrays where the registries should be, so `cargo()`, `hasCargo()`, `stow()` and `unload()` threw (civ-clone/web-renderer#228). Both are now declared `transient` on the mixin, and `Game.inject` supplies them.

`Transport(Base)` now returns a named type, `TransportClass` (`typeof Unit & TransportMixin`, whose instances are `Unit & ITransportUnit`), instead of an inferred class expression. The inferred type could not be written to the `.d.ts` (TS4094 for `Unit`'s private members, TS2742 for types reached through other packages), so the package did not compile and the committed `.js` and `.d.ts` were stale (civ-clone/web-renderer#20). `ITransportUnit` and `TransportMixin` are exported alongside it.

The standard workflow now compiles with `--force` and fails on stale or uncommitted output, as core-strategy's does. That step could not pass while `Transport.ts` failed to compile (civ-clone/web-renderer#20).

localChanges: Under Despotism, Monarchy and Communism, computer players now keep enough units in their cities to hold unhappy citizens in check with martial law, instead of taking citizens off the land to be Entertainers (#216).

log: Under a government with martial law, a city's wanted defenders (`defendersWanted`) are now the larger of the old `ceil(size / 5)` and the units martial law would use: the `MartialLaw` yields the ruleset's rules give the city now, plus its net `Unhappiness`, capped by the ruleset's limit. Production builds the unit, `Garrison` keeps it, and `PreventDisorder` then finds the city calm with fewer Entertainers (civ-clone/web-renderer#216).

The government check and the cap of four are Civ1 knowledge, in `lib/Civ1/martialLaw.ts` (`civ1MartialLawPolicy`), reached by the generic modules through the new `Knowledge.martialLaw`. `garrison`, `explorerShipFor` and `buildItemInCity` take the `Knowledge` to pass it on.

`civ1-city-happiness` applies martial law (Normal priority) before the Temple, Colosseum and Cathedral (Low), so in a city with more units than it needs, martial law calms everyone and the improvements emit nothing. Counting the `MartialLaw` yields in use then kept the surplus unit for good.

`martialLawUnitsWanted` is now the unhappiness before martial law or the improvements (net `Unhappiness` plus the `MartialLaw` and `CityImprovementContent` it already absorbs), less what the improvements can calm: the ruleset's `Cost` rules run over nothing but a crowd of unhappy citizens, as `City#yields` runs them. The answer no longer depends on which of the two the rules apply first.

Civ1's Wonders (Shakespeare's Theatre, J.S. Bach's Cathedral, Michelangelo's Chapel, the Oracle) calm citizens with a plain negative `Unhappiness`, not a `CityImprovementContent`, so the previous commit missed them: with martial law applied first, a city with Shakespeare's Theatre still wanted a unit per unhappy citizen.

`martialLawUnitsWanted` now takes the positive `Unhappiness` in the city's yields (what anything has to calm) less every negative `Unhappiness` other than `MartialLaw` that the ruleset's `Cost` rules give over a crowd of unhappy citizens.

The martial-law count was compared with `defendersIn`, which leaves out a `Fortifiable` unit with no defence, such as a Diplomat, which `civ1-city-happiness`'s martial law uses all the same. A city with two Warriors and a Diplomat for three unhappy citizens still built a fourth unit.

The two shortfalls are now separate. `defendersWanted` is back to `ceil(size / 5)` against `defendersIn`, and martial law compares `martialLawUnitsWanted` with `martialLawUnitsIn`, the units the ruleset's `MartialLaw` yields name. Production and `explorerShipFor` ask `wantsUnit` (either short). `garrison` keeps a unit if the city is short of defenders, or if `keepsOrder`: martial law uses this unit and doesn't have more units than it wants.

`getByTile` was `getBy('tile', tile)`: a copy of the whole registry, a bound function per improvement, and a scan, on every call. Movement-cost rules ask it for the tile a unit is leaving and the tile it is entering, for every step a unit or a path search considers, so late in a game it was asked over a million times per 100 turns of a registry holding hundreds of improvements. An improvement's tile is fixed for its lifetime (building registers it, pillaging unregisters it), so the `index()` from core-registry 0.1.3 keeps it current with no `reindex`. It now checks the site against `reachableTiles` first, as `pursue` has done since #12.

A `TradeRates` strategy on `AfterTurn`, registered straight after `PreventDisorder`, sets each computer player's rates for the turn ahead with v474.05's routine (OpenCivOne `F0_1ade_0006`), so the AI no longer plays the whole game at 50/50/0. `lib/tradeRates.ts` is the routine as a pure function in tenths; `lib/traits.ts` gives Mood, Policy and Ideology (-1/0/1) from the leader's traits, looked up by leader class in the game's `TraitRegistry`, with Militarism flipped so Civilized is +1.

On a player's first turn the rates start at Ideology + 3 science and 1 luxury. A city `PreventDisorder` left uncalmed for `food` or `tiles` adds one luxury step (`growth` cities don't), and when the luxury rate changes every city is calmed again. Civ1's policy reads disorder from the `CIVIL_DISORDER` pending effect and takes a city larger than 5 with as many happy citizens as unhappy ones to be on the edge.

One departure from v474.05, `LUXURY_REDUCTION_BELOW`: a luxury is taken away every 4th turn while science + tax < 10, not < 8, so luxuries fall back to 0 when nothing needs them. The original rule kept 1 or 2 luxuries for good and cost 2.8 advances and 92 gold a player over 150 turns in the arena, for no less disorder.
`Dependencies` gains `playerTradeRatesRegistry` and `traitRegistry`.

civ-clone/web-renderer#154's scope has `scienceStopped` follow v474.05 until #155 makes it personal: science 0 once the player has Robotics. Civ1's `TradeRatePolicy` now reads that from the player's research instead of always answering `false`. No 150-turn game reaches Robotics, so play is unchanged.

v474.05 sets every AI's science to 0 once it has Robotics. A player now stops only once it has every advance its leader wants (`lib/Science/wantedAdvances.ts`, by the ruleset's `WantedAdvancesPolicy`), and Civ1's `TradeRatePolicy.scienceStopped` reads that instead of Robotics alone.

Civ1's table (`lib/Civ1/wantedAdvances.ts`) is keyed by trait class: Robotics always; Militaristic adds nothing; normal militarism and a Friendly mood add Recycling and Nuclear Power; Civilized adds those and Computers, Genetic Engineering, Space Flight, Plastics, Superconductor and Fusion Power; Aggressive adds nothing. Future Technology is never wanted.

`ChooseResearch` takes the policy and picks among the wanted advances available, if any are, in the same single random draw, so the number of draws is unchanged. Once science has stopped it still answers the engine's choice from everything available.

civ-clone/web-renderer#155 lists Recycling and Nuclear Power under normal militarism and a Friendly mood only, and Civilized as adding the six advances behind the late Wonders and the spaceship. The table had read "also" as cumulative and given every Civilized leader all nine. A Civilized leader with a normal mood (Mao Zedong) now wants Robotics and the six. Lincoln and Hammurabi, being Friendly too, still want all nine.

localChanges: Computer players now settle their cities before ending the turn: when a city is about to fall into disorder, citizens are made Entertainers from its poorest tiles until it is calm, without ever starving it, and a city that did riot switches to building a Temple, Marketplace, Cathedral or Colosseum and buys what it can with up to an eighth of the treasury (#156).

log: A `PreventDisorder` strategy handles `AfterTurn`, so it runs once the player's units have moved (martial law and units away from home depend on where they stand). For each city the ruleset's `CivilDisorder` rules would flag at the next turn start, as it stands or, if it will grow then, with the extra unhappy citizen growth brings, it makes Entertainers through `library-city`'s `changeWorkedTile` from the worked tiles giving the least food, then shields, then trade, until the rules find it calm. Each pass starts by putting the previous turn's Entertainers back to work.

It never makes an Entertainer that would put the city into a food deficit, nor one needed only at the next size that would stop the city growing. A city it can't calm keeps the Entertainers that calm it as it stands (or none), and is noted with the reason (`food`, `growth`, `tiles`) in the player's memory, `uncalmedCities`, for the luxury rate (civ-clone/web-renderer#154).

A city that started the turn in disorder (`civ1-city-happiness`'s pending effect) switches to the first of Temple, Marketplace, Cathedral, Colosseum it can build, unless it has more shields in hand than that costs, and spends up to an eighth of the treasury on it, as v474.05 does: the whole purchase through `PlayerTreasury#buy` when it fits, otherwise as many shields as that buys at the ruleset's price per shield.

The generic part is `lib/City/disorder.ts`, given a `DisorderPolicy`; Civ1's is `lib/Civ1/disorder.ts`. `Dependencies` gains the specialist registries, which `civ1Knowledge.assignWorkers` now passes on.

localChanges: A computer player that has no city by its fifth turn now founds one where its Settlers stand, so no civilization sits out the game on a bad start (#207).

Computer players no longer build nothing but soldiers once they have met an enemy. Each city keeps the defenders it needs, builds attackers and explorers in proportion to the empire's size, and then builds improvements and Wonders, one Wonder at a time in the most productive city (#206).
Coastal cities build a Trireme once Map Making is known, and it explores the sea while keeping to the coast, so it isn't lost (#208).

log: A new generic strategy, FoundCapital, runs ahead of WorkerTurn. From turn 5 (a constructor parameter), a worker of a player with no city founds one where it stands, whether or not the tile passes shouldBuildCity. Before then, and once the player has a city, it does nothing and WorkerTurn looks for a good site as before.

On seed 3 the Zulu start on a one-tile island whose only tile scores 158 against shouldBuildCity's 160, so their Settlers never moved or founded a city (civ-clone/web-renderer#207). They now found it on turn 5. Every other first city in 40 arena games was founded by turn 5, so the rule changes nothing else.
The capture test removes the Settlers that building its world spawns, which would otherwise found a city and draw the Warrior back to defend it.

City production (lib/Civ1/buildItemInCity.ts) now builds each kind of unit only while the player has fewer than it wants, and otherwise falls through to Wonders and improvements (civ-clone/web-renderer#206):

Defenders: while a city has fewer units that can defend it than defendersWanted (lib/City/defence.ts), which Garrison now shares. Production wanted two units on the tile while Garrison kept one in a city under size 6, so the second walked off and the city built another: 436 of 480 choices in six games were that defender.

Explorers, new, ahead of Settlers: the cheapest land unit that can fight, while there is land to explore and fewer than 3 + 2 per city are out. The defender churn was what explored the map, and without this, explored tiles fall by 40-60%.
Attackers: while there is something to attack and fewer than 1 per city, rather than whenever an enemy city is known.
Wonders: one at a time, in the player's most productive city. The old test wanted a single Production yield over 4, but a city's yields come one per tile and unit, so it was almost never true.
The random pick no longer includes ships, which were lost at sea.
The numbers come from ProductionPolicy, which ChooseProduction asks for per player (civ-clone/web-renderer#157 can derive it from the leader's traits).
From review of the previous commit:
The attacker and explorer quotas count units the player's cities are building as well as those it has, so cities choosing in the same turn don't all build the last one wanted.

The attacker branch builds only a land unit whose attack beats its defence (the same test the quota counts by), and is skipped when there is none. With only Warriors to build, contact made every city build Warriors that never counted towards the quota.
Garrison counts the defenders on the tile (isDefender, shared with production), not every unit, so Settlers in a small city no longer stop its only Warrior from fortifying.

BuildExplorerShip, a new generic strategy ahead of ChooseProduction, builds the cheapest ship a city can when the player has more than one city, no ship and none on order, the city has its defenders, and the water beside it reaches sea the player hasn't explored (lib/City/explorerShip.ts). With Civ1's units that is a Trireme once Map Making is known (civ-clone/web-renderer#208).

Civ1's canReturnAfter now keeps a Trireme safe (lib/Civ1/trireme.ts): it moves off the coast, or attacks from there, only with a move to spare and a coastal tile beside it, so it never ends its moves off the coast, where civ1-unit loses it half the time.
Missions: exploring the sea now comes before hunting enemy units, as exploring land already did. Ahead of it, the new Triremes went after enemy ships and were sunk.

A mission skips any target the unit can't reach by land (or by sea, for a ship) before searching for a path to it (lib/Unit/reachable.ts). Once ships show the coasts of other continents, every land unit looking for a mission searched its whole continent for each of those tiles, and some games took ten times as long. Play is unchanged: the checksums of seeds 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7 are identical with and without it.
Transports and escorts to other continents aren't part of this.

From review: every known water tile beside an unknown one is a sea tile to explore, so a lake whose far shore the player hadn't seen passed the check, and a city on it could build a Trireme that could never leave. isOnSea now also wants the city's body of water to be at least 20 tiles, judged from the map, as Civ1's own AI knows the extent of each ocean. No lake arises in the 40 arena games: the numbers are unchanged.

localChanges: test: the arena reports Wonders, improvements, first-city turns and units lost at sea

Computer players now plan where to found their cities: Settlers head for the nearest good site instead of founding only where they happen to stand, and a unit keeps to its destination once it has one rather than picking a new one every turn (#199).
Computer players explore the land first, then go after enemy units they can reach, and weigh an attack by how much stronger they are (#199, #201).
A computer player that loses a city now retaliates against the player that took it, not against itself, and a city with shields to spare builds the Wonder it picks (#201).

log: The survey's three missing `!`s are fixed, so enemy units, sea tiles to explore and good city sites now reach the target board. `existingTarget` now means what the code around it needs: a tile some living unit is already heading for (its target, or the end of its path), from `claimedTiles`. The survey drops destroyed units' targets and paths first (`forgetDestroyedUnits`). `reviewCities` uses the same claims, so a city already being reinforced isn't offered to a second defender.

The mission gate in `MissionAndMove` is now "no target and no path". A unit keeps following its path instead of being given a new mission every turn. Paths still end themselves when blocked (`moveUnit` drops a path it can't follow). `attackEnemyUnits` only qualifies when there is an enemy unit on terrain the unit can cross, so a ship with only land targets goes on to explore by sea. `pursue` doesn't search for a missing target or the unit's own tile.

Settlers claim the nearest good site they have a path to, and set off along that path. A site is given up when reached, when it stops being a good site, or when the path is lost and can't be found again.

Now that enemy units reach the target board, the first-match mission order matters. With hunting ahead of land exploring, as it was written, units chased enemies instead of exploring. Over 20 arena games against d660d9b the AI then explored 167 fewer tiles (t -4.6) and researched fewer advances (t -2.0). With hunting after land exploring, nothing is worse at |t| >= 2 and cities are better (+0.78, t 2.8). Only-beatable targets, only-nearby targets and the two combined were also tried. The PR description has the tables.

`pursue` tried only the nearest candidate. When it had no path there (an enemy on another landmass, say), the mission still counted as taken, so `assignMission` stopped with the unit going nowhere. `pursue` now tries the candidates nearest first until `Path.for` finds one, and returns whether it did. Every mission returns that, so a unit with nowhere reachable falls through to the next mission.

This applies to all six missions (undefended city, liberate, enemy units, enemy cities, land and sea exploring), since they all go through `pursue`. It also covers liberation for units that can't liberate: the candidate list is empty, so the mission isn't taken.

Tests cover a farther reachable enemy chosen over a nearer unreachable one, `false` when none is reachable, a ship exploring while a city waits to be liberated, and `MissionAndMove` keeping a unit on its path when nearer targets come up.

`scoreUnitMove`'s 24-per-point margin bonus and the garrison's stronger-unit swap compared `Yield` objects with `>`. `Yield` has no `valueOf`, so both were always false. They compare `.value()` now, as the lines around them already did.

City production meant to build another defender while fewer than two units on the city's tile are fortified. The count used an inner `filter`, which returns an array, always truthy, so every unit counted. It uses `some` now.

With more than 4 shields to spend, city production picked a Wonder, then carried straight on and replaced it with the random pick. It now returns after building the Wonder. It only considers one when a Wonder is available, so `build(undefined)` can't be reached. The random draw for the Wonder is made only when one is built, so the case with no Wonder available draws one number fewer (it used to throw there). The up-front random pick is still drawn on every call, as before.
When one of its cities was destroyed, `cityLost` pushed the AI's own cities into `enemyCitiesToAttack`. It now pushes the destroyer's cities.

`unitDestroyed` now uses its `player` argument, which `Rules/Unit/defeated` passes as the owner of the unit that won. That player's units on or next to the fallen unit's tile become enemy-unit targets, the same kind of revenge as `cityLost`, before the existing emergency production runs.

`lastUnitMoves`, `unitPathData` and `unitTargetData` are keyed by unit and were never pruned. A unit destroyed in combat is now forgotten straight away, through the `Defeated` rule's call to `unitDestroyed`. Units destroyed any other way (founding a city, disbanded, lost at sea) are dropped from all three maps by the survey at the start of the owner's turn. Before, only the path and target maps were swept there.
The target lists hold tiles, not units, and the survey rebuilds them every turn. A path already heading for an enemy unit that has since died ends at its last tile, and the unit takes a new mission.
test: city production with shields to spare but no Wonder falls back without throwing

log: Initial commit
Update error text
Work in progress - core AI `Strategy` rewrite.

The standard workflow from civ-clone/web-renderer#66: Node 22, pnpm with no lock file and web-renderer's settings, and it runs the tests. prettier:check now has --check, so it fails on unformatted files instead of printing them.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.
StrategyAIClient.takeTurn is rewritten so that SimpleAIClient can extend it without changing play:
BeforeTurn and AfterTurn actions, offered once per turn to every Strategy that handles them (StrategyRegistry.attemptAll).

Mandatory actions are taken one at a time, with exactly one hasMandatoryActions() and one mandatoryAction() call per action, the same calls in the same order as SimpleAIClient.takeTurn. Each builds PlayerActions and so uses DataObject ids, and nothing else lists the player's actions.

The turn ends at the first action no Strategy handles, after an unhandledAction hook. That is how a turn ends normally: the engine's EndTurn is offered once nothing else is mandatory, and nothing handles it. Before, EndTurn kept the loop running forever, or threw UnhandledAction.
A thrown error goes to actionFailed, which can carry on, end the turn, or rethrow (the default). SimpleAIClient will use it to skip a broken unit.
actionLimit (1,000) and actionLimitReached replace the 10,000-action UnhandledAction throw, and are checked where SimpleAIClient checks its loopCheck, so it can reproduce that exactly.
Non-mandatory actions are no longer offered (they were, with Promise.all), and takeTurn no longer recurses. Offering them will be added deliberately later, because it changes play.
The RNG defaults to core-random's seeded instance, not Math.random, and the fields are TypeScript private rather than #private.
chooseFromList awaits the registry and only uses a Strategy's answer if it called choose(); otherwise it falls back to Client's random pick, unchanged.
UnhandledAction is removed, as nothing throws it now. The package gets its first tests, and depends on core-strategy 0.1.6 for the async registry.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.
CI installs with pnpm and no lock file, and nothing reads this one.
Refs civ-clone/web-renderer#66.

takeTurn's try also wrapped actionLimit, actionLimitReached and unhandledAction, so a subclass whose actionFailed carries on could swallow a failing limit hook and loop past the guard forever. Only registry.attempt is inside the try now; a throw from a hook fails the turn. The order of calls, including exactly one hasMandatoryActions() and one mandatoryAction() per action, is unchanged.

chooseFromList used registry.attempt, which only says that some strategy returned true, while the choice could have been made by an earlier strategy that returned false. It now goes through registry.ordered itself, resets the Data (new Data.reset()) before each strategy, and uses the value only when that same strategy both chose and returned true. Otherwise it falls back to Client's random pick as before.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.
The same steps as core-strategy's workflow: tsc --build --force and prettier:format, then fail if either changed a tracked file, before the tests run against the committed .js.
Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

`git diff --exit-code` only sees tracked files, so a new module whose `.js` was never added passed, and the published package would omit it. The check now fails on modified or untracked `.js`, `.d.ts` and `.js.map`, listing them, and ignores everything else, such as the lock file the install writes.
Same change as civ-clone/core-random#1. Refs civ-clone/web-renderer#66.

The registries, engine and random number generator the constructor receives are now one `Dependencies` bag (lib/Dependencies.ts), with no player in it. The seven target lists and the three per-unit maps are one `Memory` object (lib/Memory.ts) owned by the client, holding the same arrays and maps for the same lifetimes. The old field names stay as private getters, since the tests reach in for `_citiesToLiberate`.
No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

`shouldAttack`, `movesBetween` and `carriersFor` are generic modules. Aircraft fuel and whether an aircraft can get home (lib/Civ1/aircraft.ts) and the terrain judgements for cities, irrigation, mines and roads (lib/Civ1/terrain.ts) are Civ1 modules. Each takes the dependency bag and the player instead of reading the client.
No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

`preProcessTurn` now delegates to three generic modules: the target survey (lib/Turn/surveyTargets.ts), the pass over the player's cities that assigns workers and notes undefended ones (lib/Turn/reviewCities.ts), and waking aircraft aboard carriers (lib/Turn/wakeCarrierAircraft.ts). The revolution to Monarchy that starts `takeTurn` is lib/Civ1/government.ts.

Where a generic module needs a Civ1 judgement (a good city site, which tiles citizens work, whether a unit is an aircraft) it asks a `Knowledge` (lib/Knowledge.ts), which lib/Civ1/knowledge.ts supplies.
The survey's three missing `!`s are kept and marked. No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

Opening and running a negotiation with neighbouring players (lib/Diplomacy/negotiate.ts) and the answer chosen at each step (lib/Diplomacy/chooseNegotiationStep.ts) are generic modules. The awaits, the 500 ms race and the 20 ms sleep are where they were, and `chooseFromList` still settles in the same number of ticks.
No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

`moveUnit` (lib/Unit/moveUnit.ts: follow the path, else take the best-scored step) and `scoreUnitMove` (lib/Unit/scoreUnitMove.ts) are generic modules, along with standing a unit down (lib/Unit/orders.ts) and the by-name action lookup (lib/actionLookup.ts). The action and unit type classes now come from library-unit, which civ1-unit re-exports, so they are the same classes.

The random tie-break stays inside the sort comparator. The client's `moveUnit` hands back the module's promise without an extra `async`, so awaiting it takes the same ticks. No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

A unit's turn is now generic modules run in the old order: aircraft wait for carriers (lib/Unit/waitForCarrier.ts), then lib/Unit/takeUnitTurn.ts seeds the move history and runs transport unloading, a worker's tile work, garrisoning, mission assignment and the move executor. Tile work and mission assignment still fall through into the move executor.

Mission assignment (lib/Unit/assignMission.ts) is six first-match missions in priority order: undefended city, liberate, enemy units, enemy cities, explore land, explore sea. A unit that qualifies for one tries no other, even with no path, and each sorts the same list in place (or a filtered copy) as before.
`takeUnitTurn` returns the move executor's promise, or `null` when the unit acted without moving, so `takeTurn` awaits exactly where it used to. No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

What a city builds (lib/Civ1/buildItemInCity.ts) and which government to take after Anarchy (added to lib/Civ1/government.ts) are Civ1 modules. The random research pick (lib/Science/chooseResearch.ts) is generic.

City production still draws its random pick on every call, before it knows whether it'll use it. Two defects are kept and marked: the Wonder choice is always replaced by the random pick, and the count of fortified units counts every unit. No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

`cityLost` (lib/Events/cityLost.ts) and `unitDestroyed` (lib/Events/unitDestroyed.ts) are generic modules. `unitDestroyed` is handed the client's city production to run. Both still act on the same target board during other players' turns.
Kept and marked: `cityLost` targets the player's own cities, and `unitDestroyed` ignores who destroyed the unit. No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.
Sorts the module imports and imports the negotiation module for its `ChoiceMetaDataMap` entry, so the declaration keeps it for anyone reading SimpleAIClient.d.ts. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.
docs: fix typos and grammar in comments

`lib/MemoryRegistry.ts` hands out one `Memory` per player, created on first use and held in a `WeakMap`. It sits in the dependency bag, so the client and the strategies coming next reach the same arrays and maps. The client's `cityLost`, `unitDestroyed` and private getters read it through `memory()`. `createDependencies` fills the bag from the module singletons, with any of them replaced.
No change in play. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

Each concern in `lib/` gets a stateless `core-strategy` `Strategy` in `Strategies/`. Each takes the dependency bag and the ruleset's `Knowledge`, gets the player from the action and narrows `handles` to what it deals with. Generic strategies are grouped by concern (`Turn/`, `Unit/`, `Science/`, `Diplomacy/`) and Civ1 ones are in `Strategies/Civ1/`.

`registerStrategies.ts` builds the pack in today's decision order (`createStrategies`) and registers it into `game.strategies`, including `defaultGame` from `index.ts`, as `registerRules` does. It registers no `Priority` rules. The unit strategies share one per-action context (`Strategies/lib/unitTurnContextFor.ts`), so each unit's turn still reads its actions and seeds its move history once. `takeUnitTurn` builds the same context through `lib/Unit/unitTurnContext.ts`.

`SimpleAIClient` doesn't use the pack yet, so nothing plays differently. Depends on `@civ-clone/core-strategy@^0.1.6` and `@civ-clone/core-strategy-ai-client@^0.1.2`, neither published yet. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

`SimpleAIClient` keeps its name, its positional constructor and defaults, its public methods and the `Rules/` hooks. It gains an optional trailing `strategyRegistry`, defaulting to the game-wide registry that `registerStrategies` fills. The turn loop is now `StrategyAIClient`'s: `BeforeTurn`, then one mandatory action at a time, then `AfterTurn`. `chooseFromList` is its `ChooseFromList` adapter, and the base `Client` pick is the fallback. The Civ1 client overrides only the hooks, which reproduce today's handling: `actionFailed` skips a failed unit and rethrows anything else, `actionLimitReached` logs the 1,000-action diagnostics and gives `NoOrders`, and `unhandledAction` logs anything that isn't `EndTurn`.
The test setup builds a `StrategyRegistry` over the same registries it hands the client. No assertion changes.

Conformance is identical at 50 and 150 turns (checksums, RNG draws, state and DTO). test:load's saved-game hash moves from 6cb2a96f to 650ca666, because the suite saves synchronously inside `turn:start`, part-way into the first player's turn, and `StrategyAIClient` awaits sooner than the old loop did. The old client with one `await` added at the start of `takeTurn` saves 650ca666 too. Part of civ-clone/web-renderer#153.

`base-unit-type-naval-transport` was declared but never imported. `core-city-improvement` is imported only by the tests, so it moves to devDependencies. `lib/Unit/takeUnitTurn.ts` is unused now that the unit strategies run its steps, and its context is `lib/Unit/unitTurnContext.ts`.
