core-data-object@0.1.17, base-city-yield-gold@0.1.1, core-save-game@0.1.6 and base-goody-hut-gold@0.1.4.
330 packages one copy each, 101 checkouts matching, npm test green with conformance unchanged.

log: Three packages declare a class called `Gold`: this yield, `base-terrain-feature-gold`'s terrain feature and `base-goody-hut-gold`'s action. A save records a class by *name*, so `PlayerTreasury._yield` was written as `{ $class: 'Gold' }` and read back as the terrain feature.

Nothing failed at load. `getByPlayerAndType` found no treasury, threw inside `ProcessYield`, and the whole yield chain died — so a loaded game applied no production, no food and no trade, with nothing to say why. dom111 found it by playing one.

Tagged `GoldYield`; the terrain feature keeps the bare name, because it is a saved entity whose `type` and ids appear in files already written. Registered here because nothing else would: `registerClasses` names the `core-` entity classes and finds the rest through `ConstructorRegistry`s, and a city yield is in neither.
Three packages declare a class called `Gold` and a save records a class by name. See base-city-yield-gold.

`DataObject._keys` is `(keyof this)[]`, so a subclass that adds any public member is not assignable to the base: registering `base-city-yield-gold`'s `Gold` failed with '"values" is not assignable to keyof DataObject', because `Yield` has a `values()`.

The constraint was tighter than the use. This registry reads `name` and `type`, and hands `prototype` to `Object.create` for the hydrator to fill — none of which needs the prototype to be typed as a `DataObject`. Widening, so every existing caller still compiles.

A save records a class by name. Three packages declare a class called `Gold`, so `PlayerTreasury._yield` was written as `{ $class: 'Gold' }` and read back as somebody else's — and the loaded game applied no production, food or trade, because the treasury lookup threw inside `ProcessYield`. The file was byte-perfect; only playing it showed anything wrong.

`encode` now checks, at the point where the name is written and the real class is still in hand, that the name resolves back to that same class. A collision becomes a refusal to save, naming the field, rather than a game that quietly does not work. One offender in a real save: the `Gold` above.
Format 2, because format 1 files carry that ambiguous reference and cannot be resolved after the fact. They are refused with the reason rather than loaded into a game that does not work.

localChanges: The load suite asserted that a loaded game *is* the game that was saved, which was true while it applied no production, food or trade: `PlayerTreasury._yield` came back as the wrong class, the treasury lookup threw inside `ProcessYield`, and the yield chain died. The state round-tripped perfectly. Only playing showed it, and dom111 found it rather than the suite.

So the suite now plays on and requires total build progress across every city to have moved. Before the fix it sat where it was — measured: 4 to 4 across a turn where an uninterrupted run went 4 to 6.

The conformance fixture is re-baselined for the DTO alone: all three state checksums are unchanged, and the DTO moved because ids follow a type tag, so `Gold-1` reads `GoldYield-1`. The byte deltas are exactly that — 195 at turn 10 is 39 ids five characters longer. Translations read the class *name*, which has not changed.
release: gzipped saves and a sensible file name

A turn-1 save was 1.6MB of JSON, and JSON of the most compressible kind: every entity repeats the same field names and most of the file is references like `{"$ref":"Tile-1f4"}`. Gzipped through `CompressionStream` it loses 93% — measured on a real save, 838KB to 55KB — and loading detects the gzip header, so files written either way still open. Without `CompressionStream` the save is written as plain JSON: a save that cannot be written would be worse than a large one.

The name came out as `The English 16x2F09x2F2026.civ-clone.json`. i18next escapes interpolated values for HTML, so the localised date arrived as `16/09/2026`, and stripping the punctuation left `x2F` behind. The default name is built from plain parts now — civilisation, turn and an ISO date — and the sanitiser only removes what a file name cannot hold: `The English, turn 1, 2026-09-16.civ-clone.json.gz`.
Five entries: the save/load UI and the engine fixes it needed — core-turn-based-game@0.1.8, core-world@0.1.16, core-city@0.1.13, core-game@0.1.4 and core-save-game@0.1.5.
core-turn-based-game@0.1.8 (Turn.set), core-world@0.1.16 and core-city@0.1.13 (registry-shaped fields rebuilt on load), core-game@0.1.4 (injectAll) and core-save-game@0.1.5 (restores the turn).
330 packages one copy each, 99 checkouts matching and typechecking, npm test green including the new load suite, conformance unchanged.

log: Same as `World._tiles`: a registry held as a field restores as a plain array, so `city.tiles()` came back unusable.

Only the container is rebuilt. Recomputing the fat cross from the `Tiles` rule would be smaller in the file and would read the *world* — which may not have rebuilt its own tiles yet, because hooks run in no particular order. A hook that puts its own class back around its own restored state cannot depend on another one.

`inject` filled an entity's transient fields, ran its `onHydrated` hook and asserted nothing was left undefined — all three, one entity at a time. That breaks as soon as a hook reads another entity: `City` puts its `Tileset` back and `World` its tile registry, and a city reached before its world threw inside the hook, after a load that had otherwise succeeded.

`injectAll` does the three as sweeps: fill everything, then hooks, then the assertion — which has to come last, since a transient field a hook fills is not missing until every hook has run. `inject` keeps its single-entity behaviour.

Stage 1 took `#private` out of these packages so that `Object.assign` over a created prototype could restore state; the new sweeps went back in with `#` out of habit. They are methods, so nothing about saving changes — but they downlevel to WeakMap helpers, and the publish gate reads those as compiled output that predates its source, which is exactly the check that catches a stale build.
Two things a loaded game needs that only showed up once one was played rather than compared.

The turn is recorded in the file's metadata and the `Turn` is reachable from no entity, so nothing restored it: a game loaded in a fresh process resumed at turn 0 with a turn-40 world. In one process the loaded game adopted the same `Turn` object, so it looked right.
And hydration now injects through `Game.injectAll`, because `City` and `World` rebuild their registry-shaped fields in `onHydrated` and a hook may read any other entity.
The lockfile pinned 0.1.7, which predates `Turn.set`, so the package's own tests failed against the version its range asks for.

A save records the turn in its metadata, and the `Turn` is reachable from no entity, so loading had nothing to restore it from: a game loaded in a fresh process — a reloaded browser tab, which is how the renderer loads one — resumed at turn 0 with a turn-40 world. In one process it looked right only because the loaded game adopted the very `Turn` object the saved one had been counting.
The year needs nothing of its own: `Year.value()` is a function of the turn.

`World._tiles` is an `EntityRegistry` held as a field, and `core-save-game` writes one as an array of its members — the class around a collection is the one thing the format cannot record. So a loaded world arrived with a plain `Tile[]` and `tiles()` handed back an array iterator. Nothing failed at load; the first symptom was `Tileset.from` choking on pairs when something asked a tile for its surroundings, several turns into a game that had loaded fine.
Found by playing a loaded game rather than by comparing its bytes — a save can round-trip byte-identically and still restore a world nobody can play.

localChanges: The engine has been able to save and load for a while and no player could: the menu had no way in. Now "Save Game" writes a file through the browser, and "Load Game" — from the main menu or mid-game — reads one back.
A save leaves as a file rather than into browser storage: it is the player's, it outlives a cleared cache, and it moves between machines.

Loading reloads the page, handing the save over in `sessionStorage`. That is not a storage detail, it is how the engine gets a clean start: plugins register their rules when imported and those rules close over the singleton registries the running game already uses, so a save cannot be laid over a game in progress. A reload gives a new worker with nothing in it, and `src/js/Engine/loadGame.ts` puts the saved game into it — no `engine.start()`, because that is what generates a world.

Resuming picks up from the restored `currentPlayers` rather than firing `turn:start`: the save was taken part way through a turn, and `TurnStart` rules have already run for that player — firing them again would hand back the moves they had spent. A save taken between turns has an empty registry, and then `turn:start` is exactly right.

`buildPluginList.js` now also emits a manifest of package versions, which is what `save` writes into a file and `hydrate` checks it against; without one `save` refuses, since an empty manifest means "cannot check", not "nothing loaded".

`npm run test:load` plays a seeded game, saves it, and loads it in a second process through this same path — two processes, because loading needs an engine that has not started a game. A loaded game is byte-for-byte the game that was saved. Playing on from it still diverges; that is reported rather than asserted, and remains 05-engine-plan.md's last open Stage 5 criterion.

Four of the six had been true for days — round-trip identity, no-op suppression, the compatibility checks — and a fifth is superseded, since pending effects are entities and the refusal it describes is gone.

The two that remain are named as such: replay equivalence, still blocked because plugins register rules at import so a loaded game has none, and the 150-turn size, which has only ever been measured at turn 12.

The first deploy run failed at `npm test`: `Cannot find module '../plugins'`. `src/js/plugins.ts` and `translations.ts` are generated and git-ignored, and `test` ran `ts:compile` before anything generated them. It passed locally only because this checkout still had both from earlier builds — a clean checkout, which is exactly what CI is, has neither.

63 entries, generated by `npm run release:changelog` and added above 0.1.0@4607766 without touching the existing ones — 0.0.0 is still last. By the convention every release has followed, this commit carries entries up to its parent; its own arrives with the next release.
They cover the engine serialisation work end to end: saving and loading a real game byte-identically, named rules, pending effects, and the GitHub Actions deploy that publishes this commit.

civ.one is GitHub Pages serving civ-clone/civ-clone.github.io, which holds a built copy of this repository. Updating it meant building locally, running that repository's update.sh from a sibling checkout, and typing the commit message by hand.

The workflow does the same from a clean checkout: a frozen pnpm install with the settings from pnpm-workspace.yaml, `npm test` (typecheck plus the six engine suites), `npm run build`, then it mirrors `dist/` and `index.html` into the site repository and commits "Updates from build <sha> of web-renderer.", as every manual deploy has. It pushes with a write deploy key held as the CIV_ONE_DEPLOY_KEY secret.

`rsync --delete` replaces update.sh's `cp -R`, so superseded content-hashed assets are removed instead of accumulating. Release notes are still generated and committed before pushing: they are bundled, and a pipeline writing them would have to push back to main and trigger itself.

46 rules now carry an id — `civ1-city:<dir>/<file>/<what it does>`, e.g. `civ1-city:city/created/register` — so a variant can `replace`, `disable`, or order a rule `before`/`after` another by reference instead of outbidding it with a priority number.

Named for what each rule does rather than numbered by position, because a position id breaks the moment a rule is inserted above it. Rules built in a loop take the loop's class names — `${TerrainType.name}` and so on — which survive the production bundle because esbuild runs with `keepNames`.

Raises core-rule to ^0.1.5: 0.1.4 reads a leading string as a priority, so these rules throw `priority(...).value is not a function` against it. The range said `^0.1.0`, which would have let a consumer with an older lockfile install exactly that.

`446c15a` was formatted with prettier 3, which adds trailing commas to parameter lists and call arguments. This package pins prettier 2, whose `prettier:format` removes them again — so the next forced rebuild, in a publish wave or anywhere else, rewrote these files as a side effect.
Formatting only, no behaviour change. Separated from the rule ids that follow so neither diff hides in the other.

`city.player()` was read at assertion time, after `city.capture(enemy)` had reassigned it, so all three assertions compared against the enemy. It passed for years anyway: with `#private` fields two `Player`s had no enumerable state, and deep equality could not tell them apart. Stage 1 made `_id` enumerable and the assertion started meaning something.
The player is captured before the city changes hands. Inverted once to confirm it fails when it should.

`discharge(effect, ...context)` hands the handler whatever the discharger has in hand that the effect could not carry. A delayed action passes the action it performed, so completion can use the registries that action was constructed with instead of the singletons a handler registered at import reaches for.
A handler must not need it: an effect discharged after a load has only what the save held. Additive — handlers taking one argument are unaffected.

Format 1 was written with a top-level `pendingEffects` array — always empty — and `hydrate` refused a file with anything in it, because effects had no saveable shape until rules had identities. Stage 6 gave them the ordinary one: a `PendingEffect` is a `DataObject` in the `pendingEffects` registry slot, so it travels in `entities` and `registries` like everything else, and both Darwin's Voyage and the ten delayed actions round-trip that way.

So the field is gone from the type and from what `save` writes, and the refusal is gone from `hydrate`. Older files still carry `"pendingEffects": []`, which nothing reads, so the format number stays 1.

The package had a test script and no tests, so the publish gate could only report "not run" — every guarantee it makes was proved in web-renderer's suites instead, against a whole seeded game. These need nothing but a Game and a two-node entity:

encode writes entities as references, classes as names, registry fields as arrays, and round-trips maps and sets through decode; it refuses a nameless function by field path, and decode refuses a dangling reference.
save refuses without a plugin manifest, finds entities no registry lists by following references, and carries a pending effect as an ordinary entity.
hydrate restores a cycle without running a constructor, loads a format-1 file still carrying the old empty placeholder, and a re-save is byte-identical.
assertCompatible refuses an unreadable format and a missing plugin, and reports version drift instead of refusing.

Writing them found one real gap, recorded in the test rather than fixed here: `{ handler: () => {} }.handler` is not anonymous — the property key names it — so a named closure in a field is written as `{ $class: 'handler' }` and fails only on load. Closing that means checking every `$class` against the class registry at save time.
Also corrects the refusal message, which still pointed at Stage 6 for rule identity, and refreshes the lockfile, which predated three of the package's own dependencies.

The completions were closures bound to `this`, so they wrote to the registries the action was constructed with. Converting them to `PendingEffect` handlers moved them to module scope, and six of the ten swapped those registries for `…Instance` singletons. The game never noticed, because `defaultGame` is the singletons; every test with its own registries did. `civ1-unit`'s "should clear Fortified when activated" watched `Fortified` land in a registry it was not looking at.

`delayedBusy` holds the performed action, so it now passes it through `discharge`, and `registerDelayedAction` hands it to `complete` — as a third argument, not the first, so packages written against the two-argument form keep working. After a load there is no performed action, and the `action` factory rebuilds one with defaults, which is all a load can do until plugins register against a game rather than at import.
Requires core-pending-effect with discharge context.

localChanges: `core-rule@0.1.5` gave `Rule` a `private _id` for rule identity, and `DataObject` has its own. TypeScript reduces an intersection of two classes that separately declare a private member of the same name to `never`, so `DataTransferClient`'s data filter — typed to take a `DataObject` — narrowed its `instanceof Busy` branch to `DataObject & Busy` and `npm run build` failed.

The branch is live, not dead: `toPlainObject` hands a filter every field it walks, and `Unit._busy` holds a rule, which this turns into `{ _: 'Fortified' }`. So the parameter is now `DataObject | Busy`, which is what it always received. Type-only; the payload is unchanged.

It got as far as the build because nothing typechecked the renderer's own source: the test suites are bundled with esbuild, which strips types without checking them, and `civ typecheck` compiles the engine checkouts. `npm test` now runs `ts:compile` first, and the release docs say why.

`generate-changelog.mjs` read external changes from the `yarn.lock` diff, and the renderer has resolved through `pnpm-lock.yaml` since b529bae — so every entry since would have listed no engine changes. It now compares the packages resolved at a commit and its parent, from whichever lockfile each has, and looks versions up by `v0.1.x` tag before bare `0.1.x`. A missing tag records the package without a log instead of stopping the run.

Local changes follow the format the release window already renders well: a one-change-per-line message keeps every line, and a subject-and-body message drops the subject and turns each body paragraph into a bullet, with trailers removed. Version-bump commits (`0.1.5`) are left out of external logs.

`--release` (`npm run release:changelog`) adds entries for every commit after the newest one, at the top of `releases.json`, without rewriting any existing entry. `generate-changelog-combined.sh` is retired: it rebuilt the file from scratch, which would delete the hand-written `0.0.0` entry and leave a trailing comma.

Checked against history before trusting it: regenerating 8a11546 reproduced the committed file byte for byte, and 4607766 matched in 32 of 34 packages — the other two are packages marked added, where the old walker kept capturing commits past the release. A trial over the 59 commits since added 59 entries with the existing 52 untouched and no missing tags.

`docs/build-and-release.md` now describes a release end to end: publish and resolve the engine, generate the changelog (it is bundled, so before the build), build on the commit being released, and deploy through civ-clone.github.io to civ.one.

`civ compile` builds a checkout's committed output outside a publish wave, in the publish procedure's format-compile-format order. It matters more than it looks: Node resolves `.js` before `.ts`, so a package's tests run whatever was last compiled, and every civ1 suite went green with named rules in the source and none in what the tests loaded. It refuses a checkout with no local formatter rather than borrowing the renderer's prettier 2, which rewrote 58 files on its first run.

`civ lint` flags a rule registered inside an `Effect` — a closure no save can carry, which is how Darwin's Voyage lost its free advances — whether built inline or bound to a variable first, the spelling Darwin's used. Inverted against the pre-conversion source from git. `civ publish` refuses on a hit.

Tests: the isolation suite checks a delayed action completes into its own game's registry rather than the singleton — the regression six Stage 6 conversions introduced — and the save suite's `pendingEffects` refusal check is now a round trip, since effects travel as entities and the placeholder is gone.
Full reinstall rather than a partial `pnpm update`, which re-resolves only what it names. Picks up core-strategy@0.1.5, core-unit@0.1.22, base-unit-action-goto@0.1.5 and core-save-game@0.1.3.
The packument took 220s to list all four, against a versioned endpoint that answers immediately — pnpm resolves via the packument, so that is the one to wait on.

log: Same gap as `Sleeping`: `BusyRegistry` listed `Stowed` among the states a lookup covers and nothing registered it, so a unit saved aboard a transport failed to load.

`Stowed`'s criterion is `() => false` — it never clears itself; disembarking replaces the busy rule instead. So there is nothing to reconstruct and the factory is the constructor. What keeps the unit on the transport is ordinary saved state on the transport, not this rule.

The last `Busy` state with no way to be rebuilt after a load. It could not be registered before, because the path its criterion compares against was never written to the file — `StrategyNote` was not a `DataObject`, so nothing in `strategyNotes` was saved — and inventing a path on load would have sent the unit somewhere it had not been going.
Two changes make the rule reconstructible:

The note holds the remaining `Tile`s rather than the `Path`. A note is saved state now, and `encode` writes a registry held as a field as an array of its members without recording the class, so a stored `Path` would come back as a plain array with no `end()`. Everything the journey needs is `shift()`, `length` and "the last one", which an array does natively and symmetrically across a save — `moveAlongPath` only ever used the first two. `entries()` returns a copy, so the array is ours to consume.

And the criterion reads the note each time instead of closing over the path, which is what leaves nothing in the rule but the unit. It also covers the note being gone — which happens the moment the unit arrives and `moveAlongPath` unregisters it — so no note means the journey is over and the unit wakes. `Rules/Player/turn-start` already recovered that way at runtime; the rule now agrees with it.

Verified in web-renderer's save suite against a real 12-turn game: a unit put on a journey comes back still following it, the tiles come back as `Tile`s rather than `$ref` strings, ending where they ended before, and the rebuilt rule reports the journey unfinished. The round trip stays byte-identical.

`Pillage` extends `DelayedAction` and was still passing a completion callback to `super.perform`, which now takes a handler identifier. Four consumers stop compiling — `library-unit`, `simple-ai-client`, `simple-world-path` and `civ1-unit` — and at runtime a pillaging unit would register a `PendingEffect` whose handler is a stringified closure, then throw `UnknownHandlerError` when it came due.

It was missed because the grep meant to find every `DelayedAction` subclass searched `node_modules/@civ-clone/*`, which are symlinks into pnpm's store — `grep -r` does not follow symlinks and returned nothing at all. `grep -R` finds eleven, not nine. `Fortify` was missed the same way and found by the same runtime error.

`Pillaging` is new. This action had no `Busy` subclass and used the base `Busy`, which cannot go in `BusyRegistry`: it is keyed by type name, so registering the base would claim the identity for every state that never subclassed it.

`BusyRegistry` named `Sleeping` among the states a lookup covers, but nothing ever registered it. A unit saved asleep therefore failed to load with `UnknownBusyError` — correct behaviour over guessing, but the gap was mine and not the registry's.

Nothing in the rule came from the action: the criterion is "an enemy is visible from where I am" and the effect is "wake up", both read off the unit and the world. Building it inline in `perform`, closing over `this.from()` and the action's own registry, made it look like it held action state. It never did, so `sleeping(unit)` builds it the same way fresh or restored.
`Sleep` extends `DelayedAction` but never calls `super.perform`, so it owes nothing and needs no `PendingEffect` — a plain factory is the whole story.

The grant used to be a one-shot rule registered inside an `Effect`, which registered another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applied to. A closure cannot be written to a file, so a save taken between finishing the wonder and starting the next research lost the two free advances silently — the player never got them and nothing said why.

`building-complete.test.ts` covers the grant. This covers the reason it was rebuilt on `PendingEffect`: that what records the debt now reaches the file, comes back pointing at the restored research, and is still spendable.

Written in web-renderer first, because `core-pending-effect` was unpublished and this package could not install. It belongs here, and it needs no world, no plugin loader and no seeded game to make its point.

The player is deliberately left out of `game.players`: it has no civilisation, and `hydrate`'s claim-replaying pass reads one from every player in that registry. A player without one cannot occur in a real game — `civ1-player` assigns a civilisation as the player is created — so hardening that pass would only hide a genuinely broken save.

"empty at turn 8" was true, and it is also why nobody noticed that `StrategyNote` was not a `DataObject`: the slot was dispositioned as runtime state and saved nothing whatsoever. It is an entity now, and the slot carries `GoTo`'s remaining path as well as AI working memory.

`core-save-game` discovers entities by walking `DataObject`s, and a note was not one — `EntityRegistry<T = any>` has no such constraint, so a registry accepted it happily and nothing ever complained. The result was that `strategyNotes` was dispositioned as runtime state and wrote nothing at all.

Two things were losing data because of it. `GoTo`'s `Busy` criterion compares the unit's tile against the end of the path it is following, and that path is held in one of these — so a unit saved mid-journey could not be restored, and `BusyRegistry` had no way to rebuild the rule. And anything the AI wants to remember across a turn goes here, which means anything it should remember across a save has to be an entity.

`value` stays `Value = any`, but the doc now says what that actually admits: entities, scalars, plain objects, arrays, `Map`s and `Set`s all survive. A class wrapped around a collection does not — `encode` writes a registry held as a field as an array of its members and cannot record which class it was — so prefer entities and arrays of them for anything a note must keep.
Three corrections, all found by fixing `Pillage`:
There are fourteen `Busy` identities, not thirteen, and ten are delayed actions rather than eight. `Pillaging` is new.
`Sleeping` and `Stowed` were listed as covered by a lookup and had no factory registered anywhere, so a unit saved asleep or aboard a transport failed to load. Now registered by their own packages.

`GoTo` was described as "looks like the exception and is not", on the grounds that the path it follows is saved as ordinary state. It is not: `StrategyNote` does not extend `DataObject`, so despite `core-save-game` dispositioning `strategyNotes` as `'state'`, no path reaches the file and the criterion cannot be rebuilt. A unit saved mid-journey fails to load. That is the honest answer until either `StrategyNote` becomes saveable or `GoTo` keeps its path somewhere that is.

Also records why counting these by hand beats grepping for them: `grep -r` does not follow symlinks, and `node_modules/@civ-clone/*` are symlinks into pnpm's store, so `-r` for `extends DelayedAction` finds nothing whatsoever.

It took two changes elsewhere: `StrategyNote` became a `DataObject`, so the path it holds is written to the file at all, and `base-unit-action-goto` now stores the remaining `Tile`s rather than the `Path` — `encode` writes a registry held as a field as an array of its members and cannot record the class around it.

localChanges: `GoTo` was the last `Busy` state that could not be rebuilt after a load, and the fix reached across three packages — `StrategyNote` became a `DataObject`, `base-unit-action-goto` stores the remaining `Tile`s rather than the `Path`, and the busy factory is registered. This is the check that the three of them add up to a restored journey.

Built here rather than by issuing a real `GoTo`, so it does not depend on the AI happening to order one, but with the pieces `GoTo.perform` uses including its exported factory. Five assertions: the unit comes back, it is still following a path, the note is there, the tiles are real `Tile`s and not `$ref` strings ending where they ended before, and the rebuilt rule reports the journey unfinished. The round trip stays byte-identical at 6,500 entities.
`civ busy`'s `KNOWN_MISSING` is empty again, which is what the list is for — somewhere to record a gap with its reason until it is closed, not somewhere to leave it.

`rm -rf node_modules pnpm-lock.yaml` and a full install, because a partial `pnpm update` re-resolves only what it names and leaves every other parent pinned. `civ stale` had all fifteen of the wave's packages one version behind their checkouts, which means the suites that passed before this were not exercising the published artifacts at all.

log: `DelayedAction.perform`'s second argument was a completion callback and is now a handler identifier. That callback was a closure, and `Unit._busy` held a rule built around it — which is why a unit part-way through this could not be saved at all.

What is recorded instead is a `PendingEffect`: the debt the unit owes, naming the handler that discharges it and carrying the turn it comes due. The completion behaviour moves to `registerDelayedAction`, registered at import, so the closure stays in this package and the file holds a name.

`this.from()` becomes `unit.tile()` in the handler — the same tile, since `isCurrentTile` is one of this action's criteria — and the registries come from their singletons rather than from the action instance.
Verified: the conformance game's checksums are unchanged, so nine delayed actions changed mechanism without changing behaviour, and a turn-12 save now round-trips byte-identically.

`01-constraints.md` §4's one unserialisable continuation. It granted two free research completions by registering a one-shot rule that registered another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applied to — so the only record of the grant was a closure in the rule registry, and a save taken between finishing the wonder and starting the next research lost it silently. The player simply never got their advances.

What records it now is a `PendingEffect` against the player's research: "owed two completions". The rule that spends them, `Rules/PlayerResearch/started`, is registered at import like every other rule — which is also why this stops needing `ruleRegistry.register` inside an `Effect`, the pattern Stage 6 adds a lint rule against.

Partly-paid debts write the remainder back rather than discharging, because discharging forgets — and a save taken between the first completion and the second would then lose the second. The last one discharges, which removes the debt and applies it.

The test for the grant now registers the rule it depends on, which it could not before: the rule did not exist until the wonder's effect created it. That is the same lesson `civ1-city`'s suite taught — a test should declare every input it relies on.

Verified end to end in the renderer: 9/9 in `npm run test:darwins`, and the conformance checksums are unchanged. The rule-count instrument moved from 1,055 to 1,056 with `Started` going 1 → 2, which is exactly right: one permanent rule at import in place of one-shots at runtime.

A `pendingEffects` slot, per-game like everything else. It holds what the game owes its entities — a unit part-way through building a road, a player owed free research — as saveable records rather than closures.

`Game` holds a `pendingEffects` slot, so its own tests could not run until that package was published — which is why the publish gate stopped here rather than half-publishing the wave. This package tracks its lockfile, so the resolution is part of the commit.
The engine has two unserialisable continuations and they looked like separate problems:

**A delayed action.** `DelayedAction.perform` closes over `endTurn = turn.value() + turns` and a completion callback, so a unit three turns into building a road holds its remaining work entirely in a closure.
**Darwin's Voyage.** It grants two free research completions by registering a one-shot rule that registers another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applies to.

Both are the same thing: a **debt owed to a target entity**. "This unit is owed the completion of a road at turn 41." "This player's research is owed two free completions." The closures implement the debt; only the debt needs saving. `01-constraints.md` §4 took Darwin's Voyage to be the engine's one unserialisable continuation — it is one of nine, since eight unit actions go through `DelayedAction`.

**There is deliberately no trigger.** Modelling *when* an effect is due — a turn, an event, a condition — is the obvious next move and the wrong one: it would be a second, weaker scheduler beside the one the engine already has. A package registers an ordinary rule, once at import, that watches whatever it cares about and discharges the effects that have come due. Leaving timing out is exactly what lets one class cover both cases:
build road       …build-road:complete   Unit            endTurn     the Busy criterion Darwin's Voyage  civ1-wonder:darwins…   PlayerResearch  remaining   a Started rule

`handler` is a string so the closure stays in the plugin and the file holds only a name. `target` is a `DataObject` so it saves as a `$ref` and comes back as the restored instance — typed as the base class, because a debt is owed to a `Unit`, a `PlayerResearch` or anything else and nothing here needs to know which.

`discharge` unregisters *before* applying, and the test says why twice over: a handler that owes a follow-up must not have it removed by the discharge that caused it, and an effect whose handler throws must not be retried every turn for ever.

`DataObject` declares `_keys: (keyof this)[]`, and that polymorphic `this` makes no subclass assignable to the base — passing a `Unit` fails on `'player' is not assignable to keyof DataObject`. The public interface says everything this needs and has no such problem.
Stage 6 of the engine serialisation plan, and the answer to 02-design-review.md §3: "208 `Rule` subclasses exist across the tree. Not one rule instance has a name, an id, or a declared origin."
`Rule`'s constructor now accepts a leading string. It is optional, so this lands package by package and the 1,055 rules a real game registers keep working untouched.

**Strings rather than subclasses, and the numbers decide it.** A real game registers 1,055 rule *instances* across 163 classes. Naming an instance is the thing `replace`, `disable`, `before` and `after` need, and no amount of subclassing provides it — you cannot subclass 1,055 times, and the second instance of any class is unaddressable either way. Subclasses answer "what kind of rule is this", which the engine already has and already uses well.
`RuleRegistry` gains `getById`, `replace`, `disableById`, `enableById`, `before` and `after`.

**`before`/`after` reposition rather than compute a priority.** Giving a rule `target.priority() - 1` looks simpler and is wrong twice: `Normal` is 2000 for almost everything, so "one less" collides with whatever else sits there, and it breaks silently when the target's priority later changes. Position is what `before` means, so position is what gets set — after the existing priority sort, which `Array.prototype.sort` keeps stable. Rules with no constraint take an early return, so the hot path is exactly as cheap as before.

**Every id-taking method throws on an unknown id.** A plugin that means to replace `civ1-city:city/grow` and mistypes it should fail at load, not run a game where its override silently never applied — which is the failure mode strings invite and the reason to guard it. Two rules claiming one id is refused at registration for the same reason `ClassRegistry` refuses two classes: the loser would be unaddressable.

The test for two rules constrained against one target caught a real bug: inserting each at `index + 1` made the second land before the first, so they came out reversed. They are grouped and spliced as a unit now, with priority deciding within a group.

The publish gate reported it: "a forced rebuild reformats 3 file(s); the commit is what gets published". The emitted `.js` and its map described the pre-prettier source, because this package was built before the format-compile-format ordering was applied to it — the same drift that 23 of Stage 4's commits carried, and that `lib/procedure.js` and `tools/stage4.js` were both changed to prevent.

Behaviour is identical either way; the artifact simply did not match the `.ts` beside it, which is exactly the kind of thing that survives every gate. A second format-compile-format pass now changes nothing.

**A real game now saves and loads byte-identically.** Turn 12 of the conformance game: 6,499 entities, 23 registries, 57KB gzipped; saved, loaded into a fresh game, saved again, and the two files are identical. That is the check that catches a dropped field, and it passes.
Three pieces made it work.

`pendingEffects` is a saved registry. The debts are entities; the handlers that discharge them are functions registered at import and are never saved, which is the whole point — a closure cannot be written to a file.

`Unit._busy` encodes as `{ $busy: '<class>' }`. It is the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — measured: 1,055 registered rules, 4,007 reachable entities, two fields. A rule is a closure, but *which* rule is a name, and every `Busy` subclass carries no instance state: anything that varies, like when a delayed action finishes, now lives in a `PendingEffect`.

`hydrate` resolves those markers in a pass of its own, after the fill. Rebuilding one needs the entity that holds it, and `decode` walks a field's value with no idea whose field it is. The order matters: the pending effects are filled by the pass before, so a factory asking when a road finishes can read it.
`$busy` is a distinct marker rather than a `$class` because a class reference decodes to the class, and what a unit needs back is an *instance*, built for it by the package that owns it.
`test:save` is wired into `npm test` now that it passes, and the registry-membership assertion compares a summary rather than printing several thousand ids on every run.

`Unit._busy` is the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — measured: 1,055 registered rules, 4,007 reachable entities, exactly two fields, both `<Unit>._busy`. A rule is a closure, so `core-save-game` refuses to encode one, and that single field is what blocks saving.

`BusyRegistry` maps a `Busy` identity to a factory that rebuilds it for a unit. A factory rather than the class, because construction is where the meaning is: `Fortified` is built with `new Criterion(() => false)` at the call site, `Stowed` builds its own, and `GoTo`'s criterion closes over the unit and its path.

This covers five of the thirteen `Busy` subclasses — `Fortified`, `Fortifying`, `Stowed`, `Sleeping`, `GoTo` — whose criteria are pure functions of the world and the unit, and whose durable facts are saved separately. `Fortify` registers a `Fortified` *`UnitImprovement`* alongside the busy rule, and that is ordinary state.

**It cannot cover the other eight, and the class comment says so rather than leaving someone to find out.** They come from `DelayedAction.perform`, which closes over `endTurn = turn.value() + turns` and the completion `action`. `endTurn` says when the work finishes; `action` says what it does. Neither is derivable from the unit, so a factory would have to invent a completion turn — and a unit three turns into building a road would load either finished or never finishing.

That is the same problem `PendingEffect` exists for: a delayed action *is* "at turn N, do X", which is exactly the handler-plus-data shape 03-save-format.md defines. Darwin's Voyage was taken to be the only unserialisable continuation in the engine. It is one of nine.

`DelayedAction.perform` took a completion callback and now takes a handler identifier. That callback was a closure, and `Unit._busy` — the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — held a rule built around it. `core-save-game` refused to encode it, so a unit three turns into building a road could not be saved at all.

`perform` now registers a `PendingEffect` carrying the turn the work comes due, and `delayedBusy` builds the `Busy` rule from *that*. One function, called from two places — `perform` when the action starts and `BusyRegistry` when a save is loaded — because if the two built the rule separately they would drift, and the drift would only appear in a loaded game.

`registerDelayedAction` pairs the two registrations a package needs: the handler that says what finishing does, and the factory that rebuilds the in-progress rule. Split across two call sites they would be easy to half-do, and a package with a handler but no factory produces a unit that loads idle while still owing the work. The action is rebuilt by a factory rather than `new ActionType(...)` because the constructors genuinely differ — `ClearForest` takes a `TerrainFeatureRegistry` where `BuildIrrigation` takes a `Turn`.

**One latent bug fixed on the way.** The criterion compared `turn.value() === endTurn`, so a unit whose completion turn slipped past — a skipped turn, or a save loaded on a later turn — stayed busy for ever with nothing to say why. It is `>=` now, which cannot get stuck and agrees on the turn it is due.
Conformance is unchanged across the nine delayed actions, and a turn-12 save round-trips byte-identically.

It mattered more than a tie-break. This was the only claimant in a registry, so a save naming `Research` resolved to the *trade rate* regardless of what it meant.

Ids key on the tag, so this entity's ids become `ResearchTradeRate-N`. That is the only behavioural difference anywhere, confirmed by normalising ids out of a turn-50 DTO dump and comparing: `_` still reports `Research`, so the renderer and the `trade-rate` translation namespace are untouched.
`registerUnitImprovements` fills the new `AvailableUnitImprovementRegistry` with `Fortified` and `Veteran`, following the same ruleset-registers-them convention as `registerAvailableBuildItems`.
`Fortified` was one of three entity types in a real save that resolved to no class at all.

`registerTileImprovements` fills the new `AvailableTileImprovementRegistry` with the five this ruleset offers, following `registerTerrainFeatures` — the ruleset registers them, not each `base-tile-improvement-*` package.
Nothing held these classes before. A save records `Irrigation` and `Road` by name and hydration could not resolve either.
The three things `core-save-game` needs from here, per Stage 5 of the engine serialisation plan.

**`typeNameOf(Class)`** returns an explicit `static type` when a class declares one and `constructor.name` otherwise, and `idProvider` now keys on it. Identical behaviour today — nothing declares a tag — which is what makes it safe to land alone, and it means ids follow the tags whenever 02-design-review.md §7 rolls them out. That rollout is 303 classes across 243 packages, so it is deliberately not a prerequisite for saving.

It reads an *own* `type`, not an inherited one. `static` members are inherited, so `Class.type` on a subclass of a tagged class returns the parent's tag — every descendant of one tagged class would save, load and take ids as that parent, an entity type swallowing a hierarchy. Caught by the test for it, and the same trap `allTransient()` walks the prototype chain to avoid.

**`idCounters()` / `restoreIdCounters()`** expose the per-class counters a save has to carry. Without them the first entity created after a load takes an id a loaded entity already holds — `City-1` twice, one of them unreachable — and nothing throws. Restoring only ever moves a counter *forward*, because plugin imports create terrain definitions, civilisations and leaders before a save is loaded, and lowering a counter would hand out ids those already hold.

**`ClassRegistry`** maps type name to class for hydration, which allocates with `Object.create(Type.prototype)` and never calls a constructor. It refuses two classes claiming one name, and refuses a name of one character — which is what `keepNames: false` would produce, and saves written then would be unreadable by any other build. §7's explicit tags are the real fix; this makes the failure a startup error instead of a corrupt file. It cannot false-positive: the shortest real class name in the engine is `Or`, at two characters, and that is a rule combinator.

`typeNameOf` is a free function rather than `static typeName()` because the static version was written first and `ConstructorStaysAssignable` rejected it immediately — a required static, method or property, stops `IConstructor<T>` satisfying `typeof T`. That is what 0.1.14 shipped, and the guard caught the second attempt within a minute.

`save.engine.plugins` needs every loaded package and its exact version, for the three-tier compatibility check in 03-save-format.md: refuse a missing plugin, allow an extra one, warn on a version change.

Nothing announced itself before this. Plugins load as bare side-effect imports from a list the host generates, so there was no manifest to read back at all. The alternative was 123 packages each registering their own name and version; instead the host that generated the import list registers the whole manifest, because it is the one place that already knows both and cannot drift out of step with the imports it wrote.

An empty manifest therefore means "cannot check", not "nothing loaded" — a distinction `core-save-game` acts on by refusing to write a save without one, rather than emitting a file that silently cannot be validated.
No tests here: this package has no runner, and adding mocha, chai and ts-mocha for two accessors is not worth it. `core-save-game`'s compatibility tests exercise them end to end.

Stage 5 of the engine serialisation plan. `stateKeys()` omits every transient field, so an entity rebuilt with `Object.assign(Object.create(Type.prototype), state)` arrives with those fields *absent* — not null, not empty, `undefined`. Measured against a real game, three of the four categories then misbehave and one does so silently:
Yield.value()          undefined   (real value 3, and no error) Tile.getNeighbours()   throws City.toPlainObject()   throws

`Yield` is the dangerous one. Its guard is `if (this._valueCache === null)`, which is false for `undefined`, so the recompute never runs and every yield in a loaded game reads empty. Nothing reports it.
So `inject` has three tables rather than the one the design assumed:

**collaborators** — registries, `turn`, `year`, and the game's `rng` for a `() => number` field. Sixteen entries, two of them spellings of the same thing (`_ruleRegistry` and `_rulesRegistry` both exist).
**caches** — the value the field's own initialiser would have produced: `[]`, `null`, `new Map()`. Five entries.

**derived** — from the game *and* the entity's restored state, so neither table can express them. `Civilization._attributes` is a filtered view of the game's; `World._generator` is rebuilt from the world's own saved height and width, which is exact because every geometry method is a pure function of those two and a loaded world never calls `generate()`.

**The assertion at the end matters more than the tables.** A transient field added later and not added here leaves `undefined` behind, so `inject` throws naming the class and the field. That is what turns the next `Yield` into a load failure instead of a wrong answer.

`_id` and `_keys` are skipped deliberately: they are transient but come from the save, beside the entity id rather than inside `state`. `_keys` cannot come from here at all — constructors build it with `addKey()`, and without it `toPlainObject()` throws and a loaded game sends nothing to the renderer.
An optional `onHydrated()` hook runs last. Exactly one class in the 328 packages needs it.

Also: a `classes: ClassRegistry` slot, per-game like everything else. It lives in `core-data-object` rather than `core-save-game` as the plan had it — that placement is a dependency cycle, since `core-save-game` depends on `core-game`.
`core-data-object` moves to ^0.1.16, the version `ClassRegistry` and `allTransient()` exist in.
Two slots, `availableTileImprovements` and `availableUnitImprovements`, alongside the existing `availableTerrainFeatures` and `availableCityBuildItems`.

They exist because nothing held the tile and unit improvement *classes* — `tileImprovements` and `unitImprovements` hold what has been built and acquired. A save records `Irrigation`, `Road` and `Fortified` by name and had nothing to resolve them against.
`core-tile-improvement` 0.1.3 → 0.1.4 and `core-unit-improvement` 0.1.2 → 0.1.3, the versions that contain `AvailableTileImprovementRegistry` and `AvailableUnitImprovementRegistry`.

`Game` imports both, so its own tests could not run until they were published — which is why the publish gate stopped here on the first pass rather than half-publishing the wave. This package tracks its lockfile, unlike most, so the resolution is part of the commit.

`PlayerTile` is the only class in all 328 packages that builds per-instance structure in its constructor: it installs an accessor per registered `AdditionalData` with `Object.defineProperty`, and calls `addKey()` with a non-literal argument. Every other class's state is either saved or supplied by the `Game`.

Those accessors are non-enumerable, so `stateKeys()` never sees them and a save never carries them. A hydrated `PlayerTile` would therefore have `_keys` naming methods that do not exist, and `toPlainObject()` walks `keys()` calling each one — so the first thing to break would be the payload sent to the renderer.

`onHydrated()` is the hook `Game.inject` calls last if a class defines one. One class needs it, so it is a hook rather than a convention. `setAdditionalData` takes a flag because the keys come back with the save and re-adding them would duplicate every one.

Stage 5 of the engine serialisation plan, implementing 03-save-format.md. `save` walks the registries holding runtime state and records every entity's non-transient fields; `hydrate` allocates each with `Object.create(Type.prototype)` — never a constructor, so nothing re-emits `city:created` — fills it, then hands it to `Game.inject` for the collaborators and caches a file cannot carry.
Measured on a real four-player 60x40 game at turn 12: **6,499 entities, 837KB of JSON, 57KB gzipped**, against a budget of 1MB gzipped at turn 150. Loading emits no creation events.
Four things here differ from the document, each for a reason:

**`ClassRegistry` lives in `core-data-object`.** The layout in the plan puts it here while `hydrate` reads it as `game.classes`, which would make `core-game` depend on this package — and this package depends on `core-game`.

**`SerialisedEntity` carries `keys` beside `id`.** `_keys` is built by `addKey()` calls inside constructors, so no `Game` can supply it, and without it `toPlainObject()` throws and a loaded game sends the renderer nothing. Putting it in `state` instead would mean removing `_keys` from `DataObject.transient`, moving the conformance checksum for something that is bookkeeping rather than state.

**Registry dispositions are exhaustive at compile time.** `registries.ts` types its table as `Record<keyof GameSlots, Disposition>`, so adding a slot to `Game` fails to compile here until someone says whether it is saved. The classifications come from measuring a real game rather than reading names: `terrainFeatures` reads like a mixed registry and is not — its definitions are classes in `availableTerrainFeatures` and every entry is a placed instance. `save` additionally refuses a `state` registry that turns out to hold a class, and `hydrate` refuses membership for a slot that is not state, because loading it would register duplicates over the definitions plugin imports already created.

**Entities are discovered breadth-first, not taken from registries.** `World` is reachable only through `Tile._map` and a `Tile` only through `World._tiles`; neither is in a `Game` registry, so a pass over the registries alone writes a save full of `$ref`s to nothing.
`pendingEffects` refuses rather than drops: restoring one needs rule identity, and silently discarding a queued continuation loses it with no symptom.
Two changes, both driven by what the acceptance test measured rather than by reading the tree.

`Yield` subclasses are constructed directly and appear in no registry, so each `core-` one has to be named explicitly. `Moves` and `FoodStorage` turned up as unresolvable entity types in a twelve-turn save; the rest are here because the next longer game would have found them one at a time.

`core-science/Yields/Research` is deliberately *not* among them, and the reason is worth recording: three classes are named `Research` — that one, `base-city-yield-research`'s byte-identical `class Research extends Yield {}`, and `base-trade-rate-research`'s `TradeRate`. Registering a fourth claimant displaces whichever got there first, which today is the trade rate. So a save naming `Research` already resolves to the wrong kind of thing, and adding to the pile makes it worse. Tags would fix it; which of the two identical `Yield`s is the real one is a modelling question, not a naming one.

`registerClasses` also takes a `collisions` array now. Throwing on the first ambiguous name made the rest invisible — there were five, and only the first was ever visible. A collected name is simply absent from the registry, so a save using it fails to load rather than loading the wrong class, and a host can report the whole list.

Harvesting classes from definition registries is restricted to `attributes` and `traits` rather than derived from the disposition. Doing it for every definition registry reaches `rules`: 1,055 `Rule` instances whose names collide 271 times over and not one of which is ever a saved entity.
With those in place, a twelve-turn save resolves 72 of its 75 entity types. The three that remain — `Fortified`, `Irrigation`, `Road` — are `base-` packages listed in no registry at all.

Two new dispositions for `availableTileImprovements` and `availableUnitImprovements`, which is all it took for **every one of the 75 entity types in a real save to resolve** — the three that did not (`Irrigation`, `Road`, `Fortified`) were in no registry, and now are. Zero ambiguous names remain, after `RailroadAdvance` was tagged: adding the tile improvement registry made `Railroad` collide with the advance, which nothing had noticed because the class had never been registered anywhere.

`encode` now refuses a function with no name rather than writing `{ $class: '' }`. Such a thing could never be decoded, and the failure would land on whoever loaded the file rather than whoever wrote it. The message carries the field path, which is how the one case that reaches it got identified:
Cannot encode Warrior._busy._criteria._criteria.[0]._criterion

That is `Unit._busy` holding a `Busy` rule, and a rule is a closure. `05-engine-plan.md` predicted exactly this and named the fix: `busy` has to serialise as a rule *identity*, which needs Stage 6's named rules. Refusing is the deliberate choice — the alternative is a save that loads with every fortified unit silently un-fortified.
So saving is now blocked on one field, which is a better place to be than blocked on a category.

`Research` had three claimants and resolved to whichever reached a registry first — the trade rate. With `base-city-yield-research` now re-exporting `core-science`'s class and the trade rate tagged `ResearchTradeRate`, the name is unambiguous and can be registered.
257 classes, zero ambiguous names, all 75 entity types in a real save resolve.

`TileImprovementRegistry` holds the improvements that have been *built* — instances, per tile. Nothing held the classes a ruleset offers, which left them reachable only through the `Available` rule: enough to decide what a unit may build, and not enough for anything that needs to enumerate them.

Saving is what exposed it. A save records `Irrigation` and `Road` by name, and hydration had no way to turn either back into a class — they were two of the three entity types in a real save that resolved to nothing at all.
Mirrors `AvailableTerrainFeatureRegistry` exactly, including the ruleset-registers-them convention: `civ1-world/registerTileImprovements` fills it, not the five `base-tile-improvement-*` packages.

`UnitImprovementRegistry` holds the improvements a unit has *acquired*: instances, per unit. The classes — `Fortified`, `Veteran` — were reachable only through the rules that grant them, so nothing could enumerate them and a save recording `Fortified` by name could not resolve it.
Mirrors `AvailableTileImprovementRegistry`, added alongside it for the same reason.

Also reports which entity and field held an unnameable class, and dumps the full entity type list under `SAVE_DUMP_TYPES`, like the conformance suite's `CONFORMANCE_DUMP`. Where it stands: 256 classes registered, 0 ambiguous names, all 75 entity types resolve, and one field blocks the save.

The acceptance test registered classes after twelve turns and reported thirteen unresolvable entity types. Eight of them — `Aztec`, `Hammurabi`, `MoctezumaII` and the rest — were an artefact of *when* it looked: `civ1-player` unregisters a civilisation and its leader when a player claims one, so a game that has been played no longer lists them.

Registering at `engine:start`, ahead of the handler that creates players, is both what a host would do and what makes the measurement honest. The count drops from thirteen to three, and the three that remain are real: `Fortified`, `Irrigation` and `Road` are `base-` packages that appear in no registry, so nothing can reach their classes.
That is worth knowing beyond this test. Anything that enumerates classes from the constructor registries has to do it before a game starts, or it silently misses whatever the game has claimed.
Not wired into `npm test`, because it does not pass yet — 5 of 7 — and the two failures are a measured gap rather than a defect. Wiring a red suite in would either go ignored or get quietly weakened.

What passes: loading emits no creation events; an unreadable format is refused; a save needing an unloaded plugin is refused *naming it*; pending effects are refused rather than dropped; and a turn-12 save is 57KB gzipped against a 1MB budget.

What fails, and why: hydration cannot resolve 13 of the 73 entity types a real save contains. Eight are a test artefact — `Aztec`, `Hammurabi` and the other claimed civilisations and leaders are *unregistered* from the constructor registries when a player takes one, so a game that has been played no longer lists them. A cold load has them, because nothing has been claimed yet.

The other five are real: `Irrigation`, `Road`, `Fortified`, `Moves` and `FoodStorage` belong to `base-`/`civ1-` packages and appear in no registry at all. Tile and unit improvements are built by units rather than by cities, so nothing lists their classes, and `Yield` subclasses are constructed directly. `core-` packages may only depend on `core-` ones, so naming them in `registerClasses` is not available. The fix is a generated class manifest, built the way the host already generates its plugin import list.

Replay equivalence — the third property the document asks for — is not checked at all, and that is stated in the output rather than omitted. The plugin loader registers rules into `defaultGame` at import time, so a loaded game has no rules and cannot be played. Stage 3 built `register(game)` for exactly this; the generated import list just does not expose the register functions.
The round-trip identity check is written and runs as soon as hydration succeeds, and it reports *where* two saves differ rather than only that they do.

Twelve files, found by stripping each file's import statements and then looking for any remaining reference to each imported name. Each one was hand-checked before removal, and the detector reports zero afterwards.

Nothing here is behaviour: `tsc --build` is clean, `npm run build:dev` succeeds, and the engine suites are unchanged. Adds `?cheat` to the query params, which puts Reveal Map, Grant Advance and Grant Gold into the game menu. Written by dom111, and already used to build every spaceship part, launch, and arrive at Alpha Centauri — which is how `core-spaceship`'s Stage 4 declarations got exercised, including `Layout._cachedSearch`. No translations for the new keys yet.

The debug panel next to it was built with `document.createElement` and `addEventListener` throughout, ignoring the `s` and `h` helpers the rest of the UI uses. Every button repeated the same nine style assignments, and only the label, the background and the last one's bottom margin ever differed — so the five of them collapse into one `debugButton` helper built with `h(s(...))`, and `makeToggle` becomes a call to it.

Two direct-DOM uses survive on purpose, both now carrying a note so they do not get "tidied" later: the download anchor needs its `href` assigned from an object URL rather than interpolated into markup, and the hotkey listener is on `document` in the capture phase, so the debug keys fire before a focused dialog swallows them. `h(element, handlers)` expresses neither.

`hydration.ts` proves an entity can be rebuilt without running its constructor. Necessary, and not sufficient — it hand-writes the state it hydrates from, including `_keys`, so it never exercised what a real save would actually omit.

This rebuilds live entities from a real game exactly as the hydrator's passes 1 and 2 do — `stateKeys()` for the state, `_id` and `_keys` carried beside it — then injects and calls the accessor that broke:

Yield.value()                   3          (was undefined, silently) Tile.getNeighbours()            works      (threw) City.toPlainObject()            works      (threw) City.keys()                     works      (undefined) World.get()                     works      (no generator was saved) Civilization.attributes()       works      (a derived registry) PlayerTile.toPlainObject()      works      (accessors reinstalled)
15 checks, wired into `npm test`. Two of them are worth calling out:

`Year.value()` asserts *parity with the original* rather than a value. A bare `Game` has no `YearRule`, so the original throws too — asserting a number would have been asserting the fixture rather than the behaviour, and the contract here is that a hydrated entity behaves as the one it was rebuilt from.

The last check inverts the guard: a class whose `transient` names a field `inject` has no source for must make the load fail, naming the field. It asserts on the message, so a throw for the wrong reason does not pass.

Writing this found two defects in itself rather than in `inject` — a `Year(turn, ruleRegistry)` constructor called with the arguments the wrong way round, and a `City` whose player had no civilisation, which `toPlainObject()` reaches for and throws on. Both worth noting because both looked like hydration failures at first.
Three findings, each measured against a real game rather than reasoned about, by rebuilding live entities from `stateKeys()` alone — exactly what the documented hydrator's passes 1 and 2 produce.

The design assumed every transient field is "a registry the `Game` holds". The Stage 4 declarations disagree: they also contain caches, `DataObject` bookkeeping, and one class's derived accessors. `transient` means "not saved", which is a wider category than "supplied by the `Game`".

Caches need their *initialiser*, not a collaborator, and the guards are written against it — `if (this._valueCache === null)` is false when the field is absent, so `Yield.value()` returns `undefined` with no error and every yield in a loaded game reads empty. `Tile.getNeighbours()` and `Year` fail the same way but throw. So `inject` needs a table of five empties, and more importantly an assertion that no transient field is left `undefined` — which is what turns a future cache field into a load failure rather than a wrong answer.

`_keys` cannot be injected at all: it is built by `addKey()` calls inside constructors, and without it `toPlainObject()` throws, so a loaded game sends nothing to the renderer. It belongs beside `id` in `SerialisedEntity`, not in `state` — putting it in `state` would mean removing it from `DataObject.transient`, which moves the conformance checksum for something that is bookkeeping rather than state.
`PlayerTile` is the only class in 328 packages that builds per-instance structure in its constructor. One class, so one optional `onHydrated()` hook rather than a convention.

Also recorded for Stage 5: why `ClassRegistry` went into `core-data-object` rather than `core-save-game` (the documented placement is a dependency cycle), and why §7's `static type` is not a prerequisite — 303 classes across 243 packages, 210 uncloned, against a failure mode `ClassRegistry` can refuse outright for one method's worth of code.

25 packages, 9 waves, all verified live on the registry and pushed with tags. Full re-resolve rather than `pnpm update`, per 04-package-workflow.md: one copy of each of the 328 packages, every installed copy matching its checkout.

Conformance unchanged against the published artifacts: aebaf5c2 / af0ade7e / f6e495ff, 9/9 hydrated, 13/13 isolated, 27/27 transient. The DTO digest — the renderer's actual transport payload — is byte-identical at all three checkpoints (788 / 3,245 / 53,120 objects, 8.9MB at turn 50, hashes 67d92604 / c27f4b32 / 40a7e611), as are the 1,055 rules across 65 types.

log: Stage 4 of the engine serialisation plan. Every field of a `DataObject` is saved unless the class says otherwise, and some of them must not be: a registry, an `Engine`, a random number generator and a cache are either supplied by the loading `Game` or derived from what it supplies, and restoring one restores a stale answer at best.

`static readonly transient` lists them. The set is derived from the field types rather than hand-written — a field typed with a registry class, with a type the `Game` holds, or with `() => number` is transient by construction, and a cache is matched by name because it has no distinguishing type. Stages 2 and 3 were mechanical for the same reason.

The dependency on core-data-object moves to ^0.1.15 because that is the first version the declaration is both read and safe in. Against an older one it is legal TypeScript that compiles to an unread static, so the field would be saved regardless and nothing would report it; 0.1.14 reads it but declared the static as required, which stopped `IConstructor<T>` satisfying `typeof T` and broke the typecheck of 22 of the 83 checkouts.
This changes nothing yet: `stateKeys()` has no callers until the save format lands, and `toPlainObject()` is unaffected, so the conformance checksums and the DTO digest are both unchanged.

localChanges: `core-data-object@0.1.14` added one required static to `DataObject` and stopped 22 of the 83 checkouts typechecking. Nothing in `core-data-object` failed: its own tests passed either side, the publish gate ran them, the renderer's suites stayed green because esbuild does not typecheck, and the conformance checksums did not move. The defect lived entirely in two call sites in other packages.

Every other gate here is per-package, so none of them could see it. `civ typecheck` compiles each checkout against the renderer's installed tree — the one place all 328 packages resolve — in about a minute.

It rebuilds with `--force` and then restores each checkout, so it refuses to run against a tree with modified tracked files rather than reverting work it did not cause. Three pre-existing failures are listed by name with the reason and the version they were verified against, and a package that starts passing is reported so a stale entry cannot hide the next real one — the rule `KNOWN_FAILING_TESTS` earned.

The last Stage 4 item, in a commit that does nothing else — which is the point. `7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b` held unchanged through Stages 1, 2 and 3, and that is exactly what let each of them claim it changed nothing. Widening ends that comparability, so the discontinuity gets one cause and this message is it.

New baseline: `aebaf5c2 / af0ade7e / f6e495ff`, from 2,459 entities and 9,729 fields at turn 1 rising to 2,490 and 9,970 by turn 50, via `DataObject.stateKeys()`. Deterministic across runs and across processes.

`snapshots.*.state` records the entity and field counts beside the hash, so a drift says how much moved rather than only that something did. Demonstrated by removing `_ruleRegistry` from `City`'s declaration — the failure Stage 4 exists to prevent: turn 10 goes from 9,793 fields to 9,796 and turn 50 from 9,970 to 9,976, one per city, with turn 1 untouched because no city exists yet. Every other part of the snapshot is identical under that change, which is why the narrow subset could not have caught it.

References are by id, because `City._tile` reaches the `World` and through it every tile. Anything that is neither a primitive nor a `DataObject` reduces to its class name — honest rather than complete, and those fields (`Unit._busy`, `Unit._status`, `PlayerTreasury._yield`) are the ones waiting on Stage 6's named rules.
The instruments stay outside the hash as before: the DTO digest, `mathRandomCalls` and the rule counts. `state` is inside it, because it is not an instrument — it is the measurement.

Same defect as `lib/procedure.js` had, reintroduced by writing a new driver: it compiled and then formatted, so the emitted `.js` and its map described the pre-prettier source. ts-morph writes `static readonly transient = ['_a', '_b', '_c'];` on one line and prettier wraps it past 80 columns, so 23 of the 24 rollout commits held a `.js` with the one-line array against a `.ts` with the wrapped one.

Harmless in itself — the same array either way — and that is the point: it compiles, it tests, it publishes, and the artifact simply does not match its source. The 23 commits have been rebuilt and amended, and a second format/compile/format pass over all 24 now changes nothing.

`tools/stage4.js` applies the transient codemod across the 24 packages, raises each one's core-data-object range to the version the declaration is read in, compiles, formats, syncs and commits. `--all` asks the codemod which packages have something to declare rather than reading the manifest, which records work *remaining* and so shrinks as the rollout proceeds.
Two codemod corrections, both found by reviewing the derivation against the source rather than against itself:

`CACHE_NAMES` was `_(.*Cache|cached.*|neighbours)`, which needs a character before a capital `Cache` — so it matched `_yieldCache` and `_valueCache` but not a bare `_cache`. `core-game-year`'s `Year._cache` is a turn-to-year memo and was classified as state.

`World._generator` is a `Generator`, which the `Game` supplies through `generators` but which only `implements IGenerator` — so it can be neither saved as an entity reference nor rebuilt from one. The obvious generalisation is wrong: `City` is also a member of a `Game` registry and `CityGrowth._city` must certainly be saved. The difference is that `City` is a `DataObject`, so this is a judgement per type and there is an explicit list of one. `Rule` descendants are deliberately not on it: `Unit._busy` is equally unsaveable but is real state, and wants Stage 6's rule identities rather than being dropped.

`tests/engine/transient.ts` is the acceptance check. A declaration is a list of strings, so nothing about it proves the field exists or that `stateKeys()` acts on it — a typo reads correctly and does nothing. It asserts on real instances that the names are real fields, that `allTransient()` stays additive across the prototype chain, that state survives, and that `stateKeys()` is narrower than `Object.keys()` at all. Verified by spelling `_neighbours` the American way and watching two checks fail.
Conformance unchanged: 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b, 9/9 hydrated, 13/13 isolated, 27/27 transient.

The wave published cleanly (civ1-city 0.1.2, civ1-city-improvement 0.1.3, core-data-object 0.1.14, all verified against the registry and the pushed tags). Reinstalling the renderer against it exposed two tree problems, both of which had been quietly true for several stages.

`civ duplicates` finds any @civ-clone package with more than one live copy, by store entry rather than by version — the duplicated copies are often the *same* version, which is what made this invisible. Two copies are two modules, so a class from one is never `instanceof` the same class from the other, and nothing reports it. `civ publish` now runs it first and refuses on a hit, since `resolutionOf` reads that tree to decide npm-versus-git-push.

`civ stale` compares each installed copy against its checkout. This one found a false claim of mine: the committed lockfile pinned `core-turn-based-game@0.1.6` and `civ1-player@0.1.1` — the commits immediately before each `registerEvents` change — so every suite run cited as Stage 3 evidence used pre-change copies of exactly the two packages that stage's second half touched. With them installed the checksums are still 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b and isolation is 13/13, so the change is behaviour-preserving; it is now measured rather than assumed. It defaults to every checkout, not the manifest, which records work *remaining* and lists 18 of 84.

The cause of both was this document's own post-wave step, `pnpm update '@civ-clone/*'`. A partial update re-resolves only what it names, and each publish of a GitHub-resolved package changes its tarball hash, so the renderer had accumulated three `civ1-city` tarballs, one per stage that published it. Replaced with a full re-resolve.

Also recorded: `npm publish` can return 202 Accepted with "being processed", so the registry 404s the new version for a minute. That is a third state beyond the two the gate knows, and `release()` pipes npm's stdio — read ~/.npm/_logs, not the wave log.
